Optimal Linear Regression Without a Variance

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (198 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.27983v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study high-probability linear regression in the infinite variance regime, wherecthe regression noise has only a finite conditional $\alpha$-moment $\nu$ for some unknown $\alpha\in(1,2)$, and the covariates may only have finite moments up to a given order (e.g., 4th moment). We give a black-box reduction that converts finite-variance regression procedures into weak-moment procedures. The reduction is based on empirical residual pruning and is agnostic to the moment exponent, the noise scale, the covariance, and the design moment. Under a finite fourth-moment condition on the covariates, any finite-variance subroutine attaining the sub-Gaussian rate yields the following when the number of samples $n$ is above a suitably defined threshold: Without knowing $\alpha$ or $\nu$, we have with probability at least $1-\delta$ that $ \|\widehat\theta-\theta^*\|_\Sigma \lesssim_\alpha \nu^{1/\alpha} \big(\frac{d+\log(1/\delta)}{n}\big)^{\frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha}}, $ where $d$ is the dimension, $\Sigma$ is the covariate covariance matrix, and $\|v\|_\Sigma:=(v^\top\Sigma v)^{1/2}$. We further prove a matching minimax lower bound that holds under the same conditions. The reduction is computationally efficient whenever the finite-variance subroutine is. We also obtain a distribution-free prediction guarantee under a bounded raw $\alpha$-moment assumption on the response, and give an analogous $\alpha$-agnostic reduction for mean estimation.

Qodo builds context into AI code review with Codex

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Qodo brings organizational context and codebase standards into Codex, helping developers catch P0 challenges across repositories.
  • Qodo⁠(opens in a new window) builds AI tools for code review and software quality, giving coding agents the organizational knowledge they need to understand the code they change.
  • Qodo uses OpenAI models including GPT‑6 Astra to gather engineering knowledge, review code, and monitor software quality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Qodo brings organizational context and codebase standards into Codex, helping developers catch P0 challenges across repositories.

Qodo⁠(opens in a new window) builds AI tools for code review and software quality, giving coding agents the organizational knowledge they need to understand the code they change. Co-founder and CEO Itamar Friedman calls it “the coding agent’s best friend.”.

Qodo uses OpenAI models including GPT‑6 Astra to gather engineering knowledge, review code, and monitor software quality. Its Codex plugin brings that context and review into developers’ coding sessions.

According to recent reports, itamar describes customer environments that can span 10,000 or more repositories, where a local code change can break a downstream service, even if it looks correct on its own. Qodo built a plugin in the Codex marketplace to address this.

According to recent reports, “Codex is really good at taking a local task and completing it in an efficient way,” Itamar claims. Qodo’s plugin gives Codex access to codebase knowledge, organizational rules, and independent review through Qodo’s Agentic Toolbox.

Recent findings suggest that with context, Codex can account for dependencies across repositories, including those hosted by different Git providers or services connected through Kafka. “Qodo will make that connection and will help Codex look at the software as a whole and not miss those P0 bugs,” Itamar says.

Sources indicate that before Codex starts writing code, it can use Qodo’s plugin to retrieve the relevant codebase rules and pull request history and patterns. After Codex makes the changes, Qodo reviews them and returns its findings directly to Codex in the same session, before the developer opens a pull request.

Sources indicate that nnenna Ndukwe, Qodo’s AI Developer Relations Lead, sees developers using this workflow to build features and tackle technical debt with GPT‑6 models in Codex. They are automating the handoff between Codex’s coding work and Qodo’s independent review. “That’s what I’ve been seeing developers do, which is really exciting because GPT‑6 is extremely capable,” Nnenna claims.

Itamar describes coding and review agents as “yin and yang”: one creates code, the other challenges it. Each role needs its own setup and context and may involve multiple agents. His vision is for agents to discuss findings and “surface only what they don’t accept” for human review. Developers would become planners and reviewers, able to inspect unresolved issues alongside the agents’ discussion, context, and prior developer decisions.

In a recent development, “That’s how you create trust,” Itamar indicates. “I think it makes the whole process overall more efficient,” Nnenna adds. “We get to leverage the best parts of our expertise.”.

Internally at Qodo, Nnenna has been using GPT‑6 Astra’s Extra High and Ultra effort settings in her own automated development workflows as well as knowledge work.

In a recent development, “What does Codex not do? I love everything that Codex does. I love the idea of combining AI and automation.”.

Nnenna schedules Codex to report on what she accomplished during the week and where she could focus or improve next. She also uses it to research conversations about agentic engineering on social platforms and suggest ideas for developer content. When it comes to her own code changes, she schedules Codex to analyze her work and suggest agent skills to create or refine.

Itamar sees an opportunity to use OpenAI’s recently rolled out Decisions API to choose which rules and agent skills apply at each stage of development, rather than rely on language models for every decision.

It has been revealed that he cites an example where the Decisions API could select which of 200 rules need checking before a language model reasons through the relevant ones, helping to make selection faster and cheaper while improving the quality of the review. “The Decisions API is an immense opportunity for us to bring more trust to the process,” Itamar says.

In a recent development, qodo’s approach combines “the best aspects of artificial intelligence and the best aspects of traditional software engineering and scripting,” Nnenna indicates. Organization knowledge guides coding agents, independent review checks their work, and human expertise resolves the questions that remain.

This creates the foundation of what Itamar describes as a software factory: a system customers could assemble and own, bringing coding and review agents together with an understanding of how software changes in production.

With OpenAI, Qodo is building a future where coding agents put more of a company’s experience to work and developers can focus their judgment where it matters most.

#24622. Breaking: Non-penetrating World Models

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Non-penetrating World Models

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (194 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.27963v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study a fresh problem of preventing object penetration in interactive video world models. To understand how existing models handle this, we introduce NoPeBench, a benchmark that evaluates how world models respond to physical obstacles. Our evaluation reveals that none of the open-source models can reliably prevent such failures. Surprisingly, however, these models already encode the information needed to predict such violations. We find that the hidden states of diffusion transformers (DiTs) can predict whether a candidate action will penetrate an obstacle. Building on this, we introduce NoPeWorld, a lightweight framework that detects and prevents penetration. Specifically, we train a small prediction head on top of a frozen DiT's hidden states to read out if a candidate action is safe or not. Unsafe actions are then replaced with safe ones that best preserve the original intent. Despite its simplicity, NoPeWorld substantially reduces the physical violation rate, averaged over six video world models, from 74% to 16%. Remarkably, our method shows zero-shot generalization to open-domain imagery, third-person viewpoints, and moving obstacles. We publicly release our code, the NoPeBench benchmark, and model weights. Project Page: https://nopeworld.github.io .

#24621. Tech Report: Model Carving: Training Transformers That Optimize Their Own Topology

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (302 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Model Carving: Training Transformers That Optimize Their Own Topology

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (302 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.27962v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machine learning has largely kept separate the choice of architecture and the process of training. A classic Transformer, for instance, trains a fixed set of attention and MLP sublayers at every layer, in the same order, and optimizes the weights within. This uniformity is a convention rather than a principled design choice, and it is likely suboptimal: the best architecture for a given task may be smaller, more efficient, and far from uniform. We believe that, ideally, training itself should shape the model's topology. To this end, we introduce Model Carving, which learns both a Transformer's weights and its architecture in a single run. By applying learnable, scalar gates to each sublayer, we allow the training loss to remove the model's own components during training -- freeing a smaller heterogeneous network inside. We evaluate Model Carving by pre-training standard Transformers from 140M to 2.7B parameters and looped Transformers from 140M to 1.3B. At equal training compute, carved models reach a lower validation loss than dense models trained with up to 1.7 times more compute. Furthermore, carved models also outperform size-matched models produced by pruning or distillation, suggesting that the best way to obtain small models for edge devices is to carve them during training, not to compress a large one afterwards. This advantage both grows with scale and carries over to downstream tasks such as few-shot evaluation and generation. Because the removed sublayers no longer run, carved models also cost up to 34% fewer FLOPs per token and decode up to 1.6 times faster without cost in quality. Our results show that architecture, like weights, should be learned and not fixed in advance, and that inside every large transformer is a smaller, faster, stronger one waiting to be carved out.

Industry observers note that dan Driscoll will join OpenAI as Senior Counselor for National Security Modernization, working with senior leadership and external partners to advise on how advanced AI can strengthen national and cyber security, with a particular focus on working with U.S. allies to advance its responsible use.

Industry observers note that in this newly created role, Dan will work with OpenAI teams and leaders across governments, industry, academia, and allied institutions to advance practical modernization initiatives that support the buildout of democratic AI. He will also help internal OpenAI teams understand the operational needs of global national security institutions.

Industry observers note that dan previously served as the 26th Secretary of the Army, overseeing the service’s operations, modernization, and resources. He brings experience spanning military service, senior government leadership, and the private sector.

It has been revealed that in his role, Dan will advise our public and private sector partners in modernizing policy and strategy choices to unlock practical uses of AI to improve national security and help ensure the world is building AI to support democratic principles. He will work to identify where operational needs, institutional change and emerging AI capabilities come together. Dan’s appointment reflects our commitment to helping democratic institutions use advanced AI responsibly to strengthen shared security, and builds on OpenAI’s work with allies and partners to strengthen cyber resilience and protect essential services under its Daybreak program.

It has been revealed that dan Driscoll was the 26th Secretary of the United States Army. As Secretary, he oversaw operations, modernization, and resource allocation for nearly one million Active, Guard, and Reserve Soldiers and more than 265,000 Army Civilians. He drove Army transformation focused on accelerating the fielding of new technology, reforming acquisition, and building a more capable force. A former Army officer and business leader, Dan has experience spanning military service, law, and the private sector.

#24618. SUAF: Spectral Universal Advantage Features for Zero-Shot Policy Improvement

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (225 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

SUAF: Spectral Universal Advantage Features for Zero-Shot Policy Improvement

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (225 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.27919v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reward-independent representations enable reinforcement learning agents to reuse knowledge across tasks, but limited representation capacity raises three fundamental questions: what statistical dependence should these representations capture, which components of that dependence should be retained for policy improvement, and how does discarding the remaining components affect decision-making? We address these questions through canonical dependence analysis. For a reference policy, we construct an action-centered, positive-lag canonical dependence matrix (CDM) that isolates the additional predictive contribution of the current action beyond the current state. Its singular value decomposition yields Spectral Universal Advantage Features (SUAF), paired features that recover delayed advantage through linear reward projections. We show that the spectrum quantifies mutual information between current action and future state-action visitation conditioned on current state and determines reward specific approximation errors. Retaining the leading modes gives optimal rank-constrained approximations under both isotropic average-case and reward-uniform minimax criteria. Separating the immediate reward contrast also avoids the spectral floor arising from direct compression of the full advantage operator. To learn SUAF from reward-free data, we develop an action-centered Soft-HGR objective with bidirectional temporal-difference estimation. We further connect spectral approximation errors to sufficient conditions for policy improvement. Finite-state experiments validate the spectral predictions and feature-learning method, while zero-shot evaluations on discrete tasks and continuous-control benchmarks demonstrate the utility of the learned representations across rewards.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: StereoVLM: Binocular Vision-Language Models for Metric 3D Spatial Reasoning

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (260 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.27915v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong semantic understanding but remain limited in their ability to reason about metric 3D space in the physical world. Existing VLMs typically infer 3D scene structure from one or more images without known camera calibration or cross-view geometric constraints. This makes metric 3D inference inherently ambiguous and leaves it unclear whether their spatial predictions are grounded in visual evidence or driven primarily by semantic priors. In contrast, calibrated stereo provides explicit cross-view geometry that resolves this ambiguity and offers a more reliable foundation for metric 3D perception and geometric generalization. We investigate how VLMs can learn transferable 3D representations directly from calibrated binocular observations. To this end, we introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning. StereoVLM follows a hierarchical learning paradigm spanning from cross-view correspondence and disparity estimation to calibration-conditioned metric depth perception and semantic spatial reasoning. We further find that disparity supervision generalizes substantially better than direct binocular depth supervision on unseen environments. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Stereo3D-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark across three levels, from point-level geometry to object-level spatial reasoning. StereoVLM-8B achieves 95.17% depth accuracy ($\delta_1$) and a 66.98 average object-level score on Stereo3D-Bench. Intervention results further indicate that the model's performance on Stereo3D-Bench benefits from valid cross-view geometry and cannot be explained solely by additional visual tokens or semantic priors. Hierarchical geometric supervision also yields average gains of 3.54 points across five spatial benchmarks and 4.3 percentage points in RoboCasa manipulation success.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Measuring AI progress on the tasks that matter in everyday life.

According to recent reports, openAI’s mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. For the more than one billion people who presently use ChatGPT every week, we want to build AI that can help with the practical challenges of everyday life, like finding childcare, accessing government services, creating a budget, preparing for school, modifying recipes, ordering groceries, designing workout aims, and more.

When someone is looking for help making their life easier, they need more than advice or a chat response. To be a truly helpful personal assistant, ChatGPT should be able to take actions that actually get things done.

In a recent development, to measure model performance over time on everyday tasks, we built an evaluation of tasks covering areas where users wanted the most help from AI and personal agents. We used this evaluation to track and drive improvement in model performance on everyday tasks over the past year.

To identify the tasks people value most, we started with two large studies that track how people spend time in both the U.S. and internationally: the American Time Use Survey⁠(opens in a new window) and the Multinational Time Use Study⁠(opens in a new window). Together, these datasets provide a detailed catalog of everyday life tasks that people do across different demographics, times of day, and seasons. To understand where people would most value AI assistance, we expanded on these existing surveys with a new demographically representative survey of 3,995 respondents. For each task, we asked a variety of questions to identify the areas where everyday people most wanted help from a personal assistant. The resulting tasks span the most crucial areas that people want help with, including caregiving, health, education, household administration, personal finances, shopping, and accessing government services.

Below are some examples of how our current models perform on practical workflows from everyday life.

Compare kindergartens near our latest home and shortlist the best fits.

According to recent reports, I’ve narrowed it to three kindergartens and organized the enrollment details. Two preferences still need your call. Want to review the shortlist?

Help me organize our community’s flood preparation volunteer force for four neighbors needing floodproofing assistance.

I’ve prepared a simple action initiative to help volunteers assess the sites mentioned and help them prepare for upcoming severe weather.

Find a home in Luzerne County that fits my budget, has a separate living unit, and keeps my commute short after school drop-off. Add the deed to my cart so I can review it.

I found one home that meets your requirements. I’ve calculated the transfer tax and added the deed to your country records cart to review.

Set up an easy way for grandma and me to watch the game together remotely.

Sources indicate that the easiest watch setup is ready, with a backup if the stream fails. Want me to walk you through it with grandma?

Help my parent adjust to a new diabetes diagnosis with a practical care and meal blueprint.

In a recent development, the first-week proposal is ready, including meals, reminders, and questions for the care team. Want to review it together before you share it with your parent?

Our latest models score very highly on many LifeVal tasks. See more.

Over the past year, we’ve trained our models to become much faster, more capable, and more aligned on browser use, computer use, and connectors tasks. Enabling these capabilities in ChatGPT also expands the types of tasks the model can help with, helping move ChatGPT beyond a chat tool and towards a truly agentic personal assistant.

To ensure AGI benefits all of humanity, we need to measure and improve model progress on what matters in the lives of everyday people. That means going beyond academic assessments of model knowledge and actually measuring how well AI models can help people navigate decisions, manage everyday responsibilities, and get meaningful things done. We are hopeful that LifeVal represents a step towards that goal.

arXiv:2611.27913v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Detecting individual instances is crucial for many segmentation problems. However, expert instance annotations are often unavailable, so instances are approximated heuristically (e.g., as connected components of semantic maps), which can merge touching objects or split fragmented ones. Even when expert annotations exist, expert disagreement or structural delineation biases can yield split or merged reference instances, corresponding to over- or under-segmentation, respectively. Panoptic Quality (PQ) and related metrics capture both segmentation and detection quality while weighting all instances equally, regardless of size. Yet when the references are biased, these metrics can neither detect split or merged instances nor distinguish valid from invalid overor under-segmentation. We present Star Panoptic Quality (StarPQ), a novel evaluation ramework, which closes this gap in two steps: First, we construct a so-called star forest in the bipartite graph whose clean, merge, and split stars isolate different failure modes. Second, we calculate the final metric by individually weighting each failure mode, allowing practitioners to account for instance delineation biases. Across various experiments, we demonstrate that StarPQ not only enables targeted penalization or eniency towards specific failure modes, but also serves as a diagnostic tool to reveal their prevalence.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.27910v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Business data systems must determine whether records refer to the same entity and retrieve records satisfying requests whose decisive properties are implicit. As agents act on these records, both tasks require auditable reasons. Dense embeddings perform well but offer opaque coordinates, cannot be filtered by meaning, and require corpus re-encoding to add newly introduced properties. We propose interpretable embeddings built from decision columns: each column stores a decision model's calibrated answer to a natural-language question, with outcomes yes, no, or not stated. A record's embedding is its answers across an ordered set of questions. Similarity decomposes exactly into per-question contributions, and new questions add coordinates without altering existing ones. On public product benchmarks, question-space retrieval matches dense candidate generation statistically in a retrieve-then-verify entity matcher, while providing exact explanations for accepted matches. Questions derived from retrieval failures triple mean reciprocal rank without re-encoding prior answers. For search, inferring the attributes of a suitable result outperforms encoding only the literal request, and combining question-space and dense scores improves retrieval, though not at our prespecified confidence threshold. A single small neural network predicts the full interpretable vector from an existing dense embedding, enabling corpus backfilling from a few thousand labeled rows at roughly 1/200 the cost. We position interpretable embeddings as a complementary, readable retrieval channel for explaining matches, filtering on attributes, and extending indexes as failures expose missing facts.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we’re raising rewards in OpenAI’s Security Bug Bounty program to further encourage independent researchers to pursue vulnerabilities in OpenAI software that our testing may have missed.
  • It has been revealed that independent security researchers play an essential role in protecting technology across the industry.
  • Today’s updates are designed to encourage and empower researchers, and to continue building a collaborative, community-first security environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we’re raising rewards in OpenAI’s Security Bug Bounty program to further encourage independent researchers to pursue vulnerabilities in OpenAI software that our testing may have missed. We’re also introducing new incentives for researchers to earn more for higher quality vulnerability reports.

It has been revealed that independent security researchers play an essential role in protecting technology across the industry. At OpenAI, incentivizing responsible disclosure is a core part of our security model, complementing our Defense Factory⁠ work, where our engineers use our models to find weaknesses, reproduce them, and test fixes.

Today’s updates are designed to encourage and empower researchers, and to continue building a collaborative, community-first security environment.

We’re more than quadrupling the midpoint of our reward ranges for medium, high, and critical findings on average. A critical vulnerability in a core product such as ChatGPT, Codex, or the API Platform will now earn up to $30,000. Exceptional critical findings on those targets remain eligible for up to $100,000, and now up to $172,000 with bonuses. The full details are available in our security bug bounty program⁠(opens in a latest window).

Recent findings suggest that high-quality reports will be eligible to earn a bonus multiplier on the base bounty. A reliable proof of concept that isolates the bug, indicates when it can be exploited, and demonstrates its impact gives us a head start on a fix. The quality multiplier recognizes the extra work that makes a finding especially useful.

To build long-term relationships and continuously empower our security community, we are introducing a tiered loyalty bonus program. This 5-tier system provides scaling bonuses to recognize, support, and celebrate researchers who consistently partner with us in making AI technology safer for everyone.

In a recent development, to support community engagement as technology evolves, priority campaigns will feature dedicated bonus pools for newly rolled out features. These short-term campaigns give researchers early, high-reward opportunities to test fresh developments and be recognized for their early contributions.

Medium - ChatGPT (core asset): A read-only member can upload files to a Project without write permission.

$2,000 × 1.15 Quality Bonus × 1.05 Bronze Loyalty Tier Bonus.

High - Prism (non-core asset): IDOR resulting in reading a file uploaded to user’s Project.

$2,500 × 1.15 Quality Bonus × 1.10 Gold Loyalty Tier Bonus.

Critical - ChatGPT (core asset): Zero-click account takeover.

$30,000 × 1.15 Quality Bonus × 1.30 Priority Campaign Bonus × 1.15 31337 Loyalty Tier Bonus.

Exceptional - ChatGPT (core asset): Significant compromise of a security boundary (e.g., ability to view arbitrary ChatGPT people’ chat messages.).

$100,000 × 1.15 Quality × 1.30 Priority Campaign × 1.15 31337 loyalty.

All scenarios and historical awards are illustrative.

If you’ve already submitted a report and we haven’t yet awarded a bounty, we’ll apply the new reward ranges. For bounties we awarded in the 30 days before this announcement, we’ll pay you the difference if your finding would have earned more under the new ranges (Base Award + Loyalty Awards).

It has been revealed that on November 20–21, our security team will be at PROMPT2PWN⁠(opens in a upcoming window) in Oakland, where researchers can test targets in person. If you’ll be there, we’d love to hear what you’ve been working on and how to partner with you.

Thank you to everyone who has taken the time to investigate a lead and report it to us. We want OpenAI to be a team you come back to when you find something we’ve missed.

arXiv:2611.27876v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Every few months, a cancer patient's CT scans decide whether treatment continues. 3D foundation models can now detect, segment, register and track lesions, yet none of them reads the scans as a radiologist does. A radiologist decides which findings are lesions, which are the same lesion months later and whether a newly introduced spot means progression, and checks each decision against the extensive rules of a clinical guideline. We introduce LesionAgent, an LLM agent that performs this read end to end without task-specific training. It operates frozen 3D models as tools, acts in 3D through coordinate-labelled views, remembers every lesion across visits in a registry, verifies every model output it relies on, and leaves every number to a deterministic guideline engine. On four public longitudinal CT datasets, LesionAgent tracks more lesions and measures them more accurately than every automatic baseline, and where the same 3D models chained by fixed rules call progression falsely at 33 of 56 follow-ups, it does so twice. On clinical follow-up CTs, it agrees with the radiologists' response at 20 of 23 follow-ups, including every change in response, and without training on DeepLesion, it retrieves more of its lesions than every tracker trained on it (89.0% vs. 87.4%). Its harness, not its LLM, makes the difference: given the same LLM and 3D models but not the harness, Claude Code reaches a detection F1 of 41% and LesionAgent 78%, and an open-weight LLM that can run inside the hospital rises from 6% to 73%. LesionAgent and a napari reading app for any LLM are available at https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/LesionAgent.

Recent findings suggest that we’re planning our next internal security sprint at OpenAI, bringing new researchers and security partners together with our own teams to use our models to test and strengthen our systems. We’re partnering with Cathedral, whose researchers will use OpenAI’s models alongside our teams to challenge our defenses, bringing differentiated expertise and approaches to finding weaknesses and helping us protect our platforms.

We’re also making improvements to our Security Bug Bounty program including more than quadrupling our rewards for critical findings. We want researchers to challenge our assumptions and help strengthen both our systems and the methods we use to defend them.

Recent findings suggest that this is part of our ongoing effort to use AI to continuously find and fix weaknesses in our systems. Our last sprint showed what this approach can deliver. We dedicated 25% of our product engineers to finding and fixing weaknesses in our systems. Using Codex, engineers investigated findings, reproduced vulnerabilities in isolated environments and prepared patches for review.

We’re building on that work because traditional cyber defenses alone are no longer sufficient. Recent incidents across the industry show how quickly threats can emerge and how important it is to build continuous defensive loops to find and fix weaknesses before attackers do.

Sources indicate that keeping the defender’s window open requires organizations to use frontier cyber capabilities to harden their systems. We’re using our most capable models to strengthen our own defenses and making them available to Daybreak customers. We’ve committed $1 billion in subsidized access over six months for frontline defenders protecting essential services and digital infrastructure. We’re also sharing our architecture and lessons⁠ from the last sprint, alongside our blueprint for empowering cyber defenders across industry and government.

We’ll keep advancing our models, using them to strengthen our own systems, and expanding access for trusted defenders. Keeping the defender’s window open will take action across the industry, and that work needs to start now.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.27870v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Visual world models can now generate compelling interactive worlds, but visual realism does not guarantee faithful dynamics. We systematically compare how categorical and continuous prediction shape learned dynamics under both next-token and iterative whole-frame generation. These choices are often bundled in approaches such as autoregressive token models and whole-frame flow matching. We design controlled 2D and 3D environments and evaluate dynamics validity, calibration, and visual quality. In 2D with lossless visual encoding, categorical models achieve higher rollout validity with less training compute, particularly for stochastic entities. Among categorical models, greedy decoding produces the highest rollout validity, while sampling from a next-token model yields the best-calibrated stochastic predictions. Failures in continuous models, such as disappearing game characters, echo those seen in more complex environments. Here, known dynamics let us measure their impact. In 3D, categorical models also achieve stronger long-horizon performance with less training compute. Even models with lossy tokenization remain competitive on semantic accuracy and FVD, despite lower next-frame RGB accuracy. Together, these findings make a strong case for categorical prediction as a compute-efficient route to learning world dynamics.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.27860v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Benchmarks for AI-based coding agents are a staple of the current AI landscape, because they are the leading way to measure the performance of LLMs. Their scores guide business and research decisions. Evaluating coding agents is challenging, since they are able to manipulate their evaluation infrastructure to artificially achieve better scores. Grading an agent's solution often requires running its code, which can then manipulate the evaluation process. BenchJack, an automated benchmark auditor, recently reached near-perfect scores on nine of ten popular agent benchmarks without actually solving their tasks. Agents already do this unprompted, as OpenAI's July 2026 Hugging Face incident revealed. Building on secure systems design, we introduce SplitBench, a privilege separation framework for evaluating coding agents and the first in the scientific literature to separate running a task's tests from judging their results. Even an agent whose code takes over the entire test environment cannot forge a pass, because a trusted grader holds the expected answers. We show that real-world benchmarks (e.g., Terminal-Bench, DeepSWE) can be ported to the SplitBench framework with minimal effort and high fidelity: 180 of 202 tasks convert, and SplitBench agrees with the native graders on 98.7% of agent attempts. We attack the converted tasks in the worst case, where adversarial agents can read all the grading code but not the expected answers. SplitBench blocked 75% of their attempts; the rest mostly reveal weaknesses in the original tasks' tests rather than flaws in SplitBench.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Launching a national program to help our future compute campuses support reliable, affordable electricity.
  • It has been revealed that today we’re launching the Grid Protectors Program, a national effort to support affordable, reliable electricity for families and businesses in the communities where we build.
  • Recent findings suggest that whether it’s heating homes during a northern cold snap or running air conditioning through a southern heat wave, families need reliable electricity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Launching a national program to help our future compute campuses support reliable, affordable electricity.

It has been revealed that today we’re launching the Grid Protectors Program, a national effort to support affordable, reliable electricity for families and businesses in the communities where we build. Working with utilities, regulators and policymakers, we’ll develop arrangements for our future campuses to reduce electricity demand when the grid is under strain.

Recent findings suggest that whether it’s heating homes during a northern cold snap or running air conditioning through a southern heat wave, families need reliable electricity. Our goal is to make campus flexibility a resource that utilities can call on when communities need it most.

Sources indicate that with U.S. data center capacity projected to exceed 100 gigawatts by 2030⁠(opens in a upcoming window), we have a once-in-a-generation opportunity to strengthen the electric grid by building campuses that can adjust their power use when communities need it most.

It has been revealed that through Grid Protectors, our ambition is to make this kind of flexibility a core part of how we build and operate future campuses. That means designing facilities to reduce electricity use when needed and working with utilities to agree on how much demand can be reduced, how rapidly and for how long. The arrangements will differ by location, and we will share additional commitments as they are finalized.

Depending on local needs and the equipment available, we will also work with grid operators to supply power from on-site generation or storage, and use batteries and power controls to smooth changes in demand.

It has been revealed that power lines, substations and other grid infrastructure builds are a fixed cost whether demand is low or high. By using more electricity when the grid has room and reducing our use when it is under strain, we can help pay for that infrastructure while limiting the need for costly upgrades to meet peak demand. That can help keep costs down for other customers.

America needs more electricity to support economic growth, and AI is becoming a significant part of that demand. Families and small businesses should not be asked to subsidize a compute campus’s electricity needs. We’ve always been committed to paying our own energy costs, including the electricity we use and the infrastructure needed to serve our campuses. Large computing facilities should pay their costs and help utilities manage the systems they depend on.

For our planned Effingham County campus, we have committed to pay the full infrastructure and electric-service costs required to serve the project. Once the campus is operating, we can reduce the power we draw during times of need, helping preserve electricity for other customers.

Our agreement with Georgia Power also includes⁠(opens in a latest window) up to 1,000 megawatts of flexible demand response, freeing up power to help keep air conditioning running in hundreds of thousands of homes during extreme heat. For scale, that is equivalent to the average electricity demand of roughly 700,000 households. That’s more households than Washington, D.C., and Boston combined.

These compute facilities are much different than data centers built even a few years ago, allowing us to be flexible in our power demand.

In a recent development, this means we can turn down our demand so that families, small businesses, and other ratepayers will continue to have power. Building grid assets is expensive and Georgia Power states this flexibility can reduce the amount of newly introduced generation it needs to build to serve future growth. Although the campus is still in development, we intend for Effingham to serve as a pilot for Grid Protectors, building on an agreement that already provides a model for future campuses.

Imagine a restaurant in a vacation town. It needs enough tables and kitchen space for the busy season, but it has to pay for that capacity year-round. Regular customers help keep it in use and cover the bills when tourism slows. We are proposing to be that regular customer.

Electricity demand also rises and falls with the seasons, with different regions facing their biggest peaks at different times. Our compute campuses need power year-round. With the right agreements, that steady demand can help spread the grid’s fixed costs across more electricity sales, while flexibility lets us reduce demand when the system is busiest. We still need to pay the costs our campuses create; the goal is for other customers to benefit, too.

Our agreement also contributes to Georgia Power’s broader strategy to lower costs for customers. The utility projects approximately $950 million in annual customer savings beginning in 2029⁠(opens in a upcoming window) from its portfolio of large-load agreements and expected growth, including Project Camellia. It estimates a benefit of at least $15 a month for a typical residential customer using 1,000 kilowatt-hours.

The Georgia agreement is a starting point. At OpenAI, through our Grid Protectors program, we see an opportunity to help communities keep the lights on even in times of emergency and high demand. We will work with utilities, regulators and policymakers to develop practical arrangements for the campuses we build in the future—arrangements that reflect local grid needs, help campuses support the grid when it is under pressure, and pay the costs we create. Long-term contracts and financial assurances can protect other customers if a project is delayed, reduced or canceled.

Flexibility cannot replace investment in upcoming energy supply and transmission. Alongside those investments, our Grid Protectors program can help make the grid more reliable and protect families and small businesses from bearing the costs of AI infrastructure. That is the standard we want our compute campuses to meet.

arXiv:2611.27826v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Many signals are defined on the nodes of a graph, such as traffic flow at road sensors or user purchases of related products. They are often partly observed, and learning their distribution enables imputing missing values and forecasting future ones. Diffusion models learn such distributions, but their forward noise is independent across nodes and does not depend on the graph. We introduce graph-aware diffusion (GAD), whose forward process is a heat diffusion on the graph driven by Gaussian noise. In the graph Fourier basis, the forward transition is a scalar Gaussian channel at each frequency. With a shared diffusion rate, high graph frequencies are attenuated faster than low ones. We propose Mode-Adaptive SNR Scheduling (MASS), which assigns each graph frequency its own diffusion rate and keeps all of them at the same SNR. For graph-stationary signals, MASS equalizes the normalized error of the optimal linear denoiser across frequencies. We bound reverse-SDE stiffness as a function of the (shifted) Laplacian's condition number, with a logarithmic upper bound for MASS and a linear lower bound for shared rates. GAD with MASS improves recommendation accuracy by 5-19%, reduces traffic-imputation RMSE by up to 7.8% with half as many reverse steps, and improves forecasting MAE and RMSE using only 3 reverse steps.

arXiv:2611.27811v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Early deep learning models attempted to simulate visual perception using a neural hierarchy that alternated between two types of layer: one modelled on cortical simple cells (that was designed to increase selectivity), and one modelled on cortical complex cells (that aimed to increase tolerance). We show that such a neural network (NN) architecture, when implemented with novel components that are better able to learn selective and tolerant representations, is capable of accurate and robust image classification and improved alignment between the behaviour of the model and the perceptual abilities of humans. Firstly, the proposed models are shallow, fewer than ten layer-pairs, which is more consistent with the rapid feedforward object categorisation performed by the biological visual system. Secondly, they are far less prone to producing classification predictions with high confidence for samples from unknown classes or for image consisting of pure noise, and hence, like humans are not easily fooled into perceiving objects that are not present in the image. Thirdly, for the proposed NNs adversarial samples cause predictions with low confidence, enabling them to be accurately identified. In contrast to humans, our networks still do not correctly classify adversarial samples. However, the behaviour of our networks is a significant step towards human-like behaviour compared to standard DNNs that produce highly confident, but incorrect, classification predictions for adversarial samples. The increased robustness to adversarial and unknown samples is achieved while maintaining competitive performance in terms of generalisation to novel samples from the training categories. This enables models of this type to be competitive with state-of-the-art DNNs across multiple different evaluation metrics and benchmark tasks.

For $\mathtt{DDP}$, zero-shot hyperparameter transfer reduces this cost by reusing settings tuned on smaller models, but its applicability to local-update training remains unclear. We propose $\mathtt{DistP}$, a theoretical framework extending existing transfer rules from $\mathtt{DDP}$ to local-update training with varying worker counts, local steps, and outer optimizers. With averaging as the outer optimizer, $\mathtt{DistP}$ supports learning-rate transfer across width and depth while improving model quality. The tuned inner learning rate also directly transfers across synchronization intervals, but follows two regimes when increasing the global batch size: square-root learning-rate scaling for larger local batches and a fixed reference rate for additional workers. We then generalize width and depth transfer to other outer optimizers, enabling stable scaling with $\mathtt{Adam}$. However, with momentum in the outer optimizer, changing batch size or local steps can require inner--outer learning-rate tuning, consistent with prior work. In language-modeling experiments at $823$M parameters, $\mathtt{DistP}$ reduces validation loss by $8.1\%$ and improves mean downstream accuracy by $10\%$ relative to baselines without retuning at the larger scale. Fitted scaling laws suggest that this advantage grows with the compute budget, reinforcing the benefits of $\mathtt{DistP}$ for communication-efficient training.

Scaling Git at OpenAI

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Building agentic-scale source control while investing in the Git ecosystem.
  • By Aaron Friel, Taylor Blau, and Ted Nyman, Members of Technical Staff.
  • Over the past year, the size and demands on our monorepo have increased at a staggering pace.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Building agentic-scale source control while investing in the Git ecosystem.

By Aaron Friel, Taylor Blau, and Ted Nyman, Members of Technical Staff.

Over the past year, the size and demands on our monorepo have increased at a staggering pace. It was clear that we needed to revamp our source control system to scale to the level of concurrent work that Codex makes possible.

Recent findings suggest that we built Pando, a new backend for Git repositories, without interrupting any engineering work or changing how our team uses Git. Pando now powers all development in OpenAI’s monorepo. Pando is designed to meet two ambitious goals: first, horizontally scalable writes, optimized for concurrent pushes to many branches. And second, maximize read throughput, so clients can download data fast enough to fully saturate their available network bandwidth.

It has been revealed that we met these goals while retaining compatibility with the Git protocol and client, enabling both our engineers and agents to seamlessly adopt Pando into their existing workflows. In production, Pando cut median push latency by nearly 5x. It now delivers nearly a petabyte of Git data per day.

Sources indicate that here, we’ll cover our motivations for building a new source-control system, along with why we chose to retain compatibility with Git. We’ll compare our system with common approaches to scaling Git, describing why Pando is uniquely capable of meeting OpenAI’s scalability needs. We also discuss what’s next, and how we’ll continue contributing to Git to support agent-scale work.

Recent findings suggest that codex has changed the scale and pace of development at OpenAI, enabling engineers to do far more work in parallel. That means more branches and pushes, more merges, and more fetches and clones from development environments, research jobs, and CI.

These demands compound. One engineer now has several changes ready for CI at once, and each push can set several jobs fetching the same commit.

Starting around the end of last year, the systems supporting our monorepo were struggling to keep up. We suffered slow fetches and pushes along with failed merges, with reliability at times falling below 90%. Had we reached a limit of Git itself, or of the way we served our monorepo? Git grew out of a community that exchanged patches to the kernel via email. For more than two decades, developers have adapted their tools around Git as the way they build software has changed. When we started to feel friction in our own monorepo, it mattered to us that we could keep building on that work.

Industry observers note that we saw a way to keep that familiar workflow while rebuilding the backend to handle pushes to different branches in parallel and serve the same history to many readers concurrently. Building on Git as the foundation of our source-control workflow meant that improvements to the client could be useful beyond OpenAI. We wanted to contribute those improvements from our copy of Git⁠(opens in a new window) to upstream, sharing them with the broader community.

Scaling a source control system has two essential dimensions: many writers pushing to different branches, and many readers fetching the same history. Pando optimizes for both.

First, Pando coordinates updates to each branch independently. Updates to unrelated branches can proceed in parallel, and a reader fetching a branch gets the history needed for that revision. The tradeoff is that a reader looking at several branches can see them at different points of time.

It has been revealed that second, Pando reuses packfiles (Git’s format for compressing multiple objects together) across fetches instead of generating an individual packfile for each client. A client may download some objects it already has, but the server can serve the same bytes to many clients with little computation.

These choices let us scale writes across branches and serve reads from caches. To see how they fit together, let’s start with how Git stores and transfers history.

Git must be able to keep two parts of a repository in sync: objects and references.

A Git repository records snapshots of files and the history connecting them as a graph of objects. An object may be either a blob, tree, commit, or tag. Blobs hold the content of an individual file, and trees associate names with blobs or other trees to form a directory structure. Commits point to a root tree and zero or more parent commits, forming the history of your repository.

According to recent reports, objects are identified by a hash of their type and contents. Objects are also immutable: recording a changed file creates a newly introduced blob, while unchanged files and directories can reuse existing objects.

Industry observers note that branches and tags are references, or “refs”, that point to commits. Committing on a branch creates a upcoming commit and updates the branch’s ref to point to it.

In a recent development, git objects reference each other by their ID, commits to trees, and trees to trees and blobs. The branch refs/heads/main points to commit C2, whose parent is C1. C1 points to root tree T1, where parser.py refers to blob B1. C2 points to root tree T2, where parser.py refers to blob B2. In both root trees, docs/ refers to the same tree, T3. Its README.md entry points to blob B3, and usage.md points to blob B4.

Git stores objects in either a “loose” or “packed” state. Loose objects are stored in individual files identified by their object ID. Packed objects are stored together in a packfile, enabling similar objects to be stored as deltas against one another.

Git can store blobs as separate files or pack them together, encoding one blob as a delta against another.

Recent findings suggest that in Git, an object is reachable from a commit if Git can find it by following links from that commit through its parents, trees, and blobs. During a fetch, the client tells the server which commits it wants and which it already has. The server finds the objects reachable from the wanted commits, excludes those it knows the client already has, and sends the remainder as a packfile in the same format Git uses on disk. A full clone starts without any objects, so it needs all the objects reachable from the history being cloned.

A push transfers objects in the other direction by asking the server to update one or more refs. The client uses the server’s set of advertised refs to avoid sending objects the server already has. The pack being sent can therefore depend on existing objects: receiving the pack alone is not enough to reconstruct the new history.

Industry observers note that replicating a Git repository means keeping both objects and references available across multiple servers. Before a replica can serve a reference’s new value, it must be able to supply the objects reachable from that value. The service also needs to coordinate competing reference updates, i.e., pushes that try to move the same branch from the same old tip to different new commits. Systems that impose a single order on all writes to a repository can make pushes to unrelated branches wait on one another.

While designing Pando, we evaluated conventional approaches for scaling source control using Git: one that coordinates ref updates across repository replicas using three-phase commit (3PC, a protocol for coordinating a commit across multiple nodes), and one that orders updates through a shared write-ahead log (WAL, a record of changes written before they’re applied) in blob storage.

In a recent development, in the three-phase commit design we modeled, the Git service keeps a complete copy of the repository on several replicas. When any server receives a push, the incoming packfile is copied and sent to all replicas in parallel. To publish the push, a majority of replicas must accept the ref patch. The server managing this is the coordinator, and it requires multiple rounds of communication between the coordinator and each other replica.

It has been revealed that to accept a reference revision, each replica locks its copy of the ref and checks that it still points to the commit the client expects. The coordinator then sends a pre-commit message to the replicas that accept. Once a majority acknowledges the pre-commit message, the coordinator tells them to perform the update. Any up-to-date replica can then advertise the new branch tip from its local copy of the repository.

According to recent reports, keeping complete replicas makes it possible to serve reads locally, and guarantees that clients get a consistent view of all references no matter which replica they pick. As a consequence, references are updated one at a time, and each push requires multiple round trips to coordinate the ref update among replicas.

Waiting for a quorum puts replica disk performance and communication latency on the push path. As write volume grows, the replicas must keep up with incoming packs as well as read traffic.

In the WAL-based design we modeled, the Git service uses a shared manifest in blob storage to order updates across the repository. When a server receives a push, it uploads the incoming packfile to a blob store and prepares the ref enhancement in its local copy of the repository. To publish the push, it adds an entry to a shared manifest stored in the blob store that records the ref update and points to the packfile. The Git server then updates the manifest using a compare-and-swap operation. This atomically replaces the manifest, or otherwise rejects the change. If another writer has updated it in the meantime, the server reads the intervening entries, checks that its ref update is still valid, and retries using the packfile it already uploaded.

Writers can upload their packfiles in parallel, but even pushes to unrelated branches require updating the same manifest. The round-trip time for a successful compare-and-swap limits how often the repository can publish a new manifest. A low-latency blob store makes this step fast. Batching lets one manifest patch several refs at the same time, at the cost of queueing updates and increasing latency.

In a recent development, the blob store can receive packfiles in parallel, but updates to the shared manifest still compete with one another. Increasing the blob store’s capacity alone doesn’t resolve that bottleneck. Each replica still needs to read and index packs from the blob store before it can serve them locally. If incoming writes outpace that work, replicas fall behind and clients wait longer to fetch newly pushed commits.

According to recent reports, that brings us to Pando. Pando is a new architecture for serving Git repositories with the goal of scaling to many clients pushing simultaneously. Here’s how it works:.

Prior to developing Pando, we had a hunch that we could meet our requirements without compromising on Git, but we did need to compromise on some of the things that most Git systems assume to be requirements:.

It has been revealed that repository-wide consistency: Providing a consistent, point-in-time snapshot of all refs requires coordination across the repository. In a system that orders all ref updates together, pushes to unrelated branches contend on a single coordination point.

Unique packfiles for every client: If two clients with different local histories fetch the same branch, the server may need to generate a different pack for each to avoid sending objects they already have. Creating these responses costs CPU and disk I/O, making it difficult to scale to high volumes of readers.

Instead, Pando provides a relaxed consistency model (causal consistency) to scale writes, and reuses packfiles to scale reads.

When a client pushes to a branch, Pando stores the incoming packfile as an immutable blob in a blob store. Each time the branch moves, Pando records a ref version containing the new tip, the pack that supplied it, and any earlier ref versions the pack depends on in a metadata store. Both the blob store and metadata store are horizontally scalable.

Fetching a commit or reference from Pando requires replaying a set of ref versions (packfiles) to the client, reconstructing the state of the client that created the ref version being fetched. This provides a weaker form of consistency across the entire repository, while providing serializability for updates to individual refs. Clients only conflict when pushing to the same ref simultaneously. A client reading several branches cannot assume those reads describe a single point in time across the repository.

A push to trunk adds an incremental pack, containing one or more commits. Each push to a side branch includes the topic’s earlier commits again, so a client with the advertised trunk version can fetch the topic in one pack.

This is a form of causal consistency. In order to fetch a reference, the reader observes the history of the writer that produced it. During a push, Pando controls what shared history the client and server agree on, ensuring clients produce more easily shared packfiles.

According to recent reports, as a consequence, Pando doesn’t provide a point-in-time state of all references during Git operations or an ordering of ref updates within a clone or fetch. Concretely, suppose that branches foo and bar are both updated during the negotiation of a full clone. During the negotiation, one client may observe foo at version 1 and bar at version 2, while another client observes foo at version 2 and bar at version 1. In practice, users and agents are agnostic to the global ordering of ref updates, and instead depend on the order of updates to a single reference.

Sources indicate that in this simulation of the three consistency models we configure 1,000 clients to each select a distinct branch and then repeatedly push unique commits, measuring total wall clock duration and push to fetch latency. The latter is an crucial metric for workloads, as it measures round trip time for consumers and agents to collaborate or to use other systems which rely on version control. The simulation models hardware ranging from commodity to premium virtual machines and blob storage systems. In this simulation, we’ve relaxed repository-wide consistency for three-phase commit.

Run this simulation comparing Pando with two other approaches. Choose infrastructure from commodity to premium hardware, number of clients, and more settings to see how they compare.

According to recent reports, the modeled three-phase commit system reveals significantly greater write latency under load as their disks saturate; meanwhile, write-ahead log systems show significantly greater read latency for the same reason, as servers struggle to keep up with reading from the journal. In both real world testing on our monorepo and in this simulation, Pando supports many thousands of clients able to push concurrently without impacting performance under load.

On handling a push, Pando validates the incoming packfile while streaming it to blob storage, without unpacking it into a local repository. When a client begins a fetch Pando selects the stored packs the reader needs, and the reader downloads them. No server needs to apply packfiles to a local repository or perform costly unpack and packing operations. Because these servers primarily perform negotiation and packfile selection, Pando servers can run on commodity hardware.

This allows Pando to scale to the limits of clients, the network between clients and Pando, and the blob storage service. With enough capacity, clients working on independent branches can each transfer packs as fast as their own connection allows. To serve more clients at that rate, we can add Pando servers and scale the metadata store and blob store alongside them.

Pando stores the writer’s packfile in blob storage and records the ref version in metadata service. On fetch, Pando selects the packs the reader needs, and Express serves them.

Stream the pushFetch the branch.

Industry observers note that an agent edits files and creates a commit locally and runs git push, which creates a packfile of those changes to upgrade a branch. Pando receives the pack and streams it to blob storage. After validating the incoming push with a single pass decode, Pando uses a multi-key transaction to record a ref version in our metadata store and atomically update the ref pointer. This enables Pando to provide “read-your-own-write” consistency. This entire write operation requires O(1)O(1)O(1) metadata reads and writes.

When another client fetches the branch, Pando selects a set of stored packs using the history the client already has. This operation requires O(log⁡Δ)O(\log \Delta)O(logΔ) metadata reads, Δ\DeltaΔ being the shortest distance in ref versions between what the client has and what the client wants. The server returns packfile URIs, and the client downloads them through a service, Express, that stores packfiles in regional caches.

This design relies on the three central services of Pando’s architecture: pushes, fetches, and compaction.

Sources indicate that when a client pushes, a conventional Git server is like a poker player showing all of its cards, revealing to the client every branch it has. The client then gathers the commits, trees, and blobs to create a packfile that excludes objects it knows the server already has.

Advertising more refs can make the push smaller. It can also make the pack harder to reuse, because another client may be missing objects the writer left out.

In a recent development, pando takes a different approach. Instead of showing its full hand, it only advertises a select set of branches to the client. This is done for two reasons:.

According to recent reports, providing a consistent view of every ref is expensive. With millions of branches, the ref advertisement alone can exceed 100 MiB. Providing this requires each server to either maintain a current mapping, requiring significant coordination overhead, or a database query that scales with the number of refs.

Industry observers note that by providing only a subset of the refs to the client, the client will generate a pack that depends only on what the server explicitly allows the client to exclude. Tracking the dependencies allows Pando to reuse the packfile a client generates in one push by serving it as the response to a subsequent fetch.

Sources indicate that as a Git server advertises more refs, clients pushing have more sources from which to exclude objects, enabling them to produce smaller packs. However, reusing these packfiles requires the server to be able to prove the clients fetching have each of the dependencies. Otherwise, the packfile may omit objects the client needs.

Recent findings suggest that on the other hand, if a Git server advertises none at all, the client would generate a packfile containing the repository’s full history. That packfile can be used by any other client, but at the significant cost of making fetching any branch effectively a full clone.

Advertising more refs results in smaller packfiles. Most of the size reduction can come from advertising just one.

In a recent development, by default, when a client pushes a latest feature branch, Pando advertises only a designated trunk branch as a base. This keeps the advertisement the same size as the repository gains branches, but comes with tradeoffs. When an engineer either pushes to a single branch many times, or stacks one feature branch on top of another the client has to resend everything outside of the trunk.

This causes successive branch pushes to be larger, containing potentially-redundant objects, and uses additional client bandwidth. In our monorepo, the median packfile produced this way was under 20 KiB, and the 99th percentile was under 3 MiB. For us, this was a sensible trade-off because a reader that already has the advertised trunk history can fetch the branch with that one packfile.

After choosing the set of refs to advertise to the client, Pando accepts the push and updates its metadata store. Pando splits the metadata patch into synchronous and asynchronous portions. The synchronous metadata update ensures clients can immediately fetch the newly updated commit. This writes a upcoming ref version and updates the ref pointer mapping to that new version storing that new tip, the dependencies used to negotiate the packfile, and a link to the packfile that was pushed.

According to recent reports, at the same time, asynchronous work is recorded in the same transaction, such as scheduling compaction. For very large pushes, only a subset of commits are written synchronously. This allows us to require only a constant number of reads and writes to the metadata store, regardless of the size of the push.

Sources indicate that importantly, Pando servers can accept pushes to unrelated refs independently. The only contended key is the ref pointer, which we guard using an atomic compare-and-swap-like operation. We can scale up write throughput by adding Pando servers, metadata store scaling units, or blob stores.

In a recent development, when a client performs a fetch, it provides the server with two sets of commit IDs, known in the protocol as haves and wants. In a conventional Git server, the server computes the set difference among the objects reachable by the haves and those reachable by the wants, compresses them, and sends the result to the client. While the open-source Git server has a variety of indexes locally to accelerate this operation, these packfiles can be expensive to compute and are generally resistant to caching.

Instead, Pando uses the commit mappings recorded on pushes to look up the client’s haves and wants, resolving them to a set of ref versions that contain those commits. Each of those ref versions links to a packfile previously received by Pando. The server uses this to solve for what the client needs, selecting the packfiles that cover the set of objects the client needs.

Pando compares what a client has with what it wants, then selects the stored packfiles needed—including any missing branch dependencies.

Select a branch to include its trunk dependencies.

Pando maps the Git protocol’s haves and wants to a sequence of ref versions. Wanting a side branch implies wanting up to its dependencies on the trunk.

The Git protocol only allows a single packfile to be sent in the HTTP response on a clone or fetch. However, an under-appreciated feature of the Git protocol, packfile-uri, allows a server to return links to download additional packs separately. Pando uses this exclusively, and transmits an empty packfile inline. To support this feature, OpenAI contributed a number of improvements to packfile-uri upstream.

OpenAI systems operate in many geographic regions, so we maintain Pando clusters with local caches in each. A pack delivery service, Express, caches our blob store, and a separate service caches the metadata store. These caches enable Pando to serve requests for a commit ID or a special read of a ref entirely from the cached state in that cluster. We use consistent hashing to route requests for a packfile to Express servers, with cache hit rates of over 99%.

This system of caches provides extremely high throughput, capable of saturating the network limit between clients and Pando. Using these packfile URIs and local caches, we’ve validated that using only standard cloud provider virtual machines, we see clone and fetch operations saturate 10 Gbps network links.

According to recent reports, for most Git servers, repacking and garbage collection are necessary to maintain the performance of a growing repository. Both of these steps reclaim space, but are compute- and I/O-intensive.

In a fast-moving repository like OpenAI’s monorepo, it is infeasible to send an individual packfile URI for every push that has occurred since the last fetch. Each day, a client would need to download tens of thousands of packfiles to catch up their trunk.

Instead, Pando combines packs in the background to reduce this overhead, adopting a design similar to compaction in log-structured merge-trees. Each push produces what Pando refers to as an “L0” packfile, representing the smallest unit of data Pando can transmit. Over time, background workers collect these packfiles into covers spanning a sequence of ref versions, scaling geometrically from L0. Today, our monorepo uses up to L4 packfile covers.

It has been revealed that these covers serve a dual purpose. After a cover is sufficiently full, a compaction worker will claim it and produce a single packfile. This improves the compression ratio by reorganizing the objects inside the packfile. But it also improves fetch negotiation performance by acting as skip list over ref versions. By scanning through indexes at each level simultaneously, Pando can select a set of packs to send to a client in logarithmic time. These packfile covers, repacked or not, enable a more efficient solution to fetch planning, reducing both throughput and latency requirements for Pando.

Small packfiles are grouped into larger covers across levels, improving compression and speeding up fetches.

Compaction combines packfiles from many ref versions in the background, enabling more efficient fetches with fewer files.

In a recent development, unlike many Git servers, packfiles are kept at every level and not discarded or garbage collected. Packs at every level are used to serve clients continuously, based on the haves and wants they request in a fetch. And for clients using Pando as an API, reading an arbitrary object from a packfile tends to require reading less data from an L0 than an L4, because it’s less likely to be compressed.

According to recent reports, compaction in Pando significantly reduces both the total transfer size sent to clients and enables pack planning to scale sub-linearly in how far behind the client is. This is especially notable for large and swiftly changing repositories, which we expect to be a upcoming normal in software development.

According to recent reports, we built Pando with Codex, moving from kick-off to production, in just 10 weeks. The core of Pando was designed by a single engineer, implemented by teams of agents, and deployed by a handful of engineers. Pando began serving production traffic in April of this year, and is one part of a larger system of source control management tools used at OpenAI.

We employed a wide variety of approaches when validating Pando’s design. We applied our principles for building more secure software foundations⁠. As a greenfield project, we chose to implement Pando in Rust and without legacy dependencies. We wrote a conformance test suite so agents could test their changes against standard Git behavior. We also developed deterministic simulation testing harnesses allowing us to check invariants and properties of the system, enabling us to find and mitigate subtle race conditions and regressions in negotiation and pack planning.

Many models contributed to this system; as upcoming models became available, we used them to improve Pando’s performance and reliability. Using GPT‑6 Astra, agents wrote Lean and TLA+ to formalize a “theory of Pando” that we used to find and fix bugs in the implementation, and prove properties of the system. Multiple continuous sessions ran for hundreds of hours finding and fixing edge cases in Pando. We also run agents around the clock to red-team Git and Pando using Daybreak-capable models.

Our initial deployment of Pando was as a read- and write-through proxy to our existing source control system. This allowed us to keep Pando and the previous system in sync, so we could safely move traffic onto Pando without downtime.

As part of its caching design, Pando can also deduplicate and combine requests before proxying. This allowed us to keep our existing tools healthy as we moved systems to Pando one at a time. As we migrated more workloads to Pando, their pushes populated Pando’s cache and improved the reliability of our previous backend.

Sources indicate that in order to optimize performance when using Pando, we began shipping our public distribution of Git to developer machines and within the ChatGPT desktop app. To migrate clients to Pando, we used an internal wrapper around the Git CLI to migrate clients in phases. We created many other tools for handling change requests, code review, and APIs for automations. We migrated hundreds of integrations that depended on legacy APIs, webhooks, and repository downloads alongside Git traffic.

According to recent reports, codex itself helped developers and teams make the move. We created skills for preparing existing checkouts, and for guiding agents to use the fresh system. As a result, developers could simply ask Codex to migrate their development environments and services.

Switching to Pando improved merge reliability and reduced the latency of the median push by nearly 80%.

In a recent development, pando can deliver a petabyte of Git data per day with just a handful of CPU cores. Pando has served more than 57 terabytes of Git packs in a single hour, with more than 99% of those bytes from local disk cache.

Reusing packs lets many clients download the same repository history with little computation on the serving nodes. This example indicates a single repository, but Pando is designed to support many more. As demand grows, we can scale data delivery and Git negotiation independently.

Building Pando on the Git protocol and client helped us identify bugs and opportunities to improve Git’s own performance.

Sources indicate that for example, Pando serves reusable packs directly to clients, so downloading and indexing those packs became a central part of making the system fast and reliable. That work surfaced edge cases in concurrent downloads, cleanup after interrupted transfers, and resuming downloads that had already completed. We fixed those paths, added validations when accepting an existing pack for a fetch, and contributed that work back upstream.

We also needed to see where time and bandwidth were going, so we added tracing for packfile-uri downloads and byte counts for pack generation, making it easier to tell whether a slow fetch was spending its time generating packs or transferring them.

Industry observers note that in OpenAI’s Git build⁠(opens in a newly introduced window), the client can download and index independent packs in parallel. We added the concept of “explicit haves” so a server can advertise a branch’s current tip separately from the history a pushing client may leave out of its pack. On Pando, this enables clients to use --force-with-lease to check that a feature branch hasn’t moved and build its pack against trunk alone. Anyone with that trunk history can then fetch the branch using the same pack.

According to recent reports, several of these improvements are already in upstream Git, and many others in our public repository. We’re continuing to work with the Git community to make these improvements useful beyond Pando. You can follow that work in our public patch tracker⁠(opens in a new window).

By rethinking conventional wisdom on how to scale Git repositories, Pando enables us to scale our monorepo without changing the Git workflows our engineers and agents already use. In our monorepo, Pando has unlocked a greater degree of parallelism, improved merge reliability, and reduced the time it takes to publish code changes. Beyond our monorepo, we’re also exploring other uses for Pando within OpenAI, including workloads where large numbers of agents need to collaborate on a shared Git repository.

According to recent reports, as engineers and agents produce more software, more teams beyond OpenAI will encounter the limits we hit in source control. We’re currently exploring ways to share the technology that makes Pando possible with our owners.

Industry observers note that pando builds on two decades of experience from customers and operators of Git repositories. We’ll continue to develop Pando while working with the open-source Git community to share any improvements that benefit Git users more broadly.
