💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, we've developed an autonomous vulnerability discovery, exploitation, and patching pipeline.
  • It has been revealed that security research that once required a separate, sustained investigation for each finding can increasingly be run as a systematic process.
  • Vulnerability discovery is becoming easier to scale, but prioritization and validation remain operational bottlenecks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we've developed an autonomous vulnerability discovery, exploitation, and patching pipeline. In one run with our cyber model, it validated and generated patches for 948 local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in Linux at an API cost of $1.2 million.

It has been revealed that security research that once required a separate, sustained investigation for each finding can increasingly be run as a systematic process. This document explores one of our efforts in this area.

Vulnerability discovery is becoming easier to scale, but prioritization and validation remain operational bottlenecks. We built a prototype to look for security flaws in the Linux kernel inside a controlled research environment. Our prototype identified and analyzed 2,308 candidate Linux kernel findings, dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities, and produced 948 local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits that could allow an unprivileged local user to gain root access.

Industry observers note that we used this evidence to prioritize vulnerabilities for reporting and developed candidate patches for maintainer review. Following guidance from the Linux kernel community, we began with critical vulnerabilities and are working with Patch the Planet partners on further reports and patches.

It has been revealed that in June, as part of our Patch the Planet initiative, we shared that GPT‑5.5 Cyber had identified Linux kernel vulnerabilities and developed 24 local privilege escalation exploits to validate and report them. We expanded that work into a pipeline, powered by an upcoming cyber model, covering vulnerability discovery, dynamic validation, exploitability assessment, and patch generation. When it finished, human researchers reviewed the outputs and reported found vulnerabilities alongside patches.

At a high level, our pipeline works as follows: first it identifies security-relevant parts of the Linux kernel, statically scans those audit targets for candidate findings, dynamically reproduces those findings in an isolated environment, creates a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit to demonstrate exploitability, generates patches, and finally a human security researcher reviews the results.

The output of the pipeline includes a root cause analysis, a minimal crashing proof-of-concept, a candidate patch, and a full exploit to assist human researchers in assessing the severity of the vulnerability and upstreaming the fixes.

Industry observers note that in a run in mid-October 2026, our pipeline using an upcoming cyber model dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities and generated PoCs for 291 information leak vulnerabilities and 948 working local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits for a commonly used Linux distribution. The total run cost $1,213,430 in API credits, or $1,279 per LPE exploit.

Sources indicate that the target virtual machines ran a stock desktop operating system, not a weakened target, under the same threat model used by cybersecurity competitions (e.g. Pwn2Own⁠(opens in a latest window), TyphoonPWN⁠(opens in a new window)). Historically, Pwn2Own and TyphoonPWN offered a $20,000 and $70,000 bug bounty for Linux kernel LPE exploits. Applying those historical bounty amounts to the 948 exploits produces a hypothetical valuation of $18.9M—$66.3M, approximately 16x to 55x our pipeline’s cost.

Sources indicate that on an adapted kernelCTF⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) environment, which is a version of the Linux kernel with reduced attack surface, our pipeline obtained 25 information leak PoCs and 21 LPE exploits. For comparison, 26 confirmed 0-day LPE exploits have been accepted by kernelCTF in 2026 at the time of writing.

In a recent development, the campaign cost roughly $32,936 in API credits. If the 21 vulnerabilities were accepted by the program, it would lead to around a $1.5M bounty award, ~45x the scanning cost.

To the best of our knowledge, the agents in this pipeline discovered and used at least 10 novel Linux exploitation techniques.

Recent findings suggest that the Linux maintainers and security community are working hard to rapidly discover and fix vulnerabilities. Within 10 days while the scan was running, we observed over 100 Linux LPEs had been patched or had staging patches from other contributors, with ~300 more being publicly discussed.

Given the rate of vulnerability discovery by frontier models, we believe automated patch generation is essential to secure software at the pace required, and to limit the exploitation window. With human expert-guided iteration, we believe AI-generated patches can be functionally correct, aligned with existing coding styles, and robust to attack variants. This is an key area for further research.

More capable models are able to discover newly introduced vulnerabilities in existing code, often including ones that have been around longer and are more complex to identify. Our analysis pipeline using the newer cyber model in mid-October discovered >5x more novel LPEs than a GPT‑5.6 Sol run in July, despite three months of hardening between the scans.

It has been revealed that large, complex software projects likely require multiple rounds of scanning and fixing vulnerabilities to “bottom out” latent bugs. Ideally this process is repeated with each subsequent generation of frontier models. This applies to both proprietary and open source software.

For the near and medium term, having access to a low-privileged account on an operating system, that isn’t up-to-date on its latest available patches should be considered functionally equivalent to root access for a well-resourced threat actor. Defense in depth, using sandboxes and isolation approaches like Firecracker and gVisor are vital for limiting the blast radius of exploited vulnerabilities.

Sources indicate that within the next few years, we believe that if there are vulnerabilities in a given software project, frontier models will likely be able to discover them and even less capable models may be able to develop exploits once disclosed. In a world of no unknown vulnerabilities, it will be critical to build and maintain high assurance software, especially core software such as operating systems, browsers, image parsing libraries, the TCP/IP stack, and more. Investing in training models to write secure code by default, minimizing attack surface by removing unnecessary features, and formal verification are promising areas of future research to effectively scale software security, in addition to finding and fixing existing vulnerabilities.

Sources indicate that the Linux kernel underpins Android devices, cloud infrastructure, supercomputers, and other systems used by billions of people. With more than 40 million lines of code, the kernel exposes a broad attack surface through system calls, networking, filesystems, and device drivers. We chose Linux to study how effectively frontier models could find vulnerabilities and demonstrate their security impact in a codebase of this scale and importance.

According to recent reports, the initial vulnerability discovery stage produced thousands of candidate findings, too many for security researchers to manually review and triage. The operational challenge of our vulnerability discovery pipeline was not discovery, but determining which findings could be reproduced, what security boundary they crossed, and which warranted the earliest maintainer attention.

It has been revealed that the mission of OpenAI’s Cyber team is to help secure the software the world relies on. We report API costs for each stage to help researchers assess the resources needed to reproduce and extend this work. These costs reflect the models, target configurations, and workflow used in this evaluation. Our broader goal is to help defenders find and fix vulnerabilities, reducing the opportunities available to attackers and raising the cost for them to exploit software.

Finally, note that we focused on methodology and measuring model capability in this research, not cost. We expect that sufficient harness engineering could meaningfully reduce the cost at each stage; thus, the costs we report are more an upper bound.

Our vulnerability research prototype is a pipeline of five stages, which uses an upcoming cyber model at its core:.

Vulnerability discovery: Agents identify security-relevant parts of the codebase and scan them for candidate findings.

Dynamic validation: Agents attempt to reproduce each candidate in an isolated environment and preserve runtime evidence. This step outputs the reproduced and validated vulnerabilities.

Exploitability assessment: Agents test whether validated vulnerabilities could enable information disclosure or local privilege escalation.

Patch generation: Agents generate patches that address each identified vulnerability.

Human review: Security researchers review the exploit, patch, and proposed severity before reporting to the maintainers.

At the end of the pipeline, the system bundles a root cause analysis, a minimal crashing proof-of-concept, a candidate patch, and a full exploit to assist human researchers in assessing the severity of the vulnerability and upstreaming the fixes.

Not every line of code in the Linux kernel is security-relevant. Our pipeline used a team of Scout agents to identify high-value audit targets, which were then passed to Analyst agents for vulnerability scanning.

Scout agents read through each folder and file and determine what targets to audit based on their reachability (reachable by low-privileged users) and security relevance.

It has been revealed that this stage identified 5,034 audit targets, about 2.8 million lines of code, which is roughly 7% of the whole Linux kernel code base, significantly reducing the cost of the security audit when compared to a full codebase analysis. This step cost $3,426 in API credits.

Next, analyst agents analyzed each audit target and produced candidate findings using a workflow similar to that of the Codex Security plugin⁠(opens in a newly introduced window). At a high level, the analyst agents read the assigned audit target’s code to understand how it works, identify its threat model, and look for vulnerabilities in it.

Within 12 hours, the analyst agents produced 2,308 candidate findings after deduplication. This stage cost $316,549 in API credits.

A candidate finding is not the same as a validated vulnerability. At this scale, manually investigating every report is impractical for our research team.

We therefore focused on validating findings that a) were reachable by a low-privileged user, b) required no special capabilities, and c) produced measurable evidence of memory corruption.

According to recent reports, for each candidate, a triage agent generated a proof of concept and ran it in an isolated virtual machine running a Linux kernel with Kernel Address Sanitizer (KASAN). The agent observed both the program output and system console, then iteratively refined the proof of concept until it reproduced the reported behavior or exhausted the potential ways of triggering it.

In a recent development, within 30 hours, our system reproduced 1724 vulnerabilities, ~74.7% of the 2,308 candidate findings. Static code review alone can be prone to false positives, so we were impressed by the accuracy of the analyst agents and the effectiveness of the triage agents in autonomously creating working proofs of concept for almost three quarters of the candidate findings.

Recent findings suggest that most remaining findings either required elevated privileges or failed to reproduce within the time budget because of difficult race conditions, specific trigger conditions (e.g., a required allocation failure at a specific line), or time-consuming validation (e.g., refcount wraparound). Only 3.1% reflected incorrect analysis by the model, where the reported vulnerability assumed an impossible condition.

According to recent reports, the validation stage cost $73,330 in API credits in total. We observed that in our validation pipeline, which needed to generate a proof-of-concept to confirm if a candidate is a real vulnerability, this process was more expensive than making a recommendation based only on static analysis, and the costs of attempting to validate a true positive and false positive were similar. Thus removing false positives earlier in the pipeline makes the process meaningfully more cost-efficient.

It has been revealed that validation establishes that a vulnerability is real, but not how urgently it should be addressed. A vulnerability that could enable local privilege escalation, for example, warrants greater priority than one that could only cause a local denial of service. With 1,724 validated vulnerabilities, the next task was to identify the findings with the greatest potential security impact.

An initial screening agent reviewed each report, crash log, and relevant source code statically. It was deliberately permissive to avoid discarding potentially serious findings, while filtering out cases without a plausible exploitation path. This narrowed the results to 313 information leak candidates and 1,238 local privilege escalation candidates.

Industry observers note that exploit-development (ExploitDev) agents then tested those candidates in isolated virtual machines configured with the protections enabled by a standard Linux distribution, including Supervisor Mode Execution Prevention (SMEP), Supervisor Mode Access Prevention (SMAP), Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization (KASLR), and HARDENED_USERCOPY. This helped prevent unrealistic assessments that depended on protections being disabled.

The agents produced 291 proofs of concept for information leaks and 1,169 working local privilege escalation exploits that could give unprivileged local users root access.

We performed variant analysis and developed 948 distinct patches for the vulnerabilities behind those exploits. We use that number to determine the overall number of unique LPEs. Successful exploits cost an average of $359 in credits to develop. That makes it relatively inexpensive for defenders to test the exploitability of found vulnerabilities.

The initial vulnerability screening agent cost $44,194 in API credits. The exploitation stage cost $775,929 in API credits in total, $84,929 for processing information leak candidates and $691,000 for local privilege escalation candidates.

Sources indicate that on average, processing a local-privilege escalation candidate ($558) was roughly two times more expensive than processing an information leak candidate ($271). This is because information leak PoCs were carried forward from the validation stage and required less modification to become usable in an exploit. On the other hand, developing an exploit from an LPE candidate required many extra steps such as exploitation strategy planning, identifying vulnerable objects to use, mitigation bypasses and more. We also noticed that unsuccessful exploitation attempts ($3,922 for 69 cases) cost much more than successful ones ($360 for 1169 cases). This was caused by a few hard-to-exploit vulnerabilities (e.g. race conditions). Defining a reasonable give-up condition, such as stopping the attempt after making no progress for one hour, would have reduced the cost of ExploitDev significantly.

Recent findings suggest that for each validated vulnerability, the system also generates a patch. We provide the model with the relevant source code and prompt it with best practices in patch writing, such as performing static checks on the patch, following the software development practices used in nearby code, and performing variant analysis to make sure the patch is complete.

It has been revealed that following the Linux kernel community’s suggestion, we have already sent out hundreds of reports and patches for critical vulnerabilities and are working with Patch the Planet partners to gradually send out patches for the rest. This work is part of our broader Daybreak commitment to support open-source projects.

In this section we share learnings, reflections, and additional analysis from this research.

Industry observers note that during this research, we observed the Linux maintainers moving quickly to fix vulnerabilities and protect users. The scan was performed on the latest Linux kernel in mid-October 2026. When the autonomous scan and manual analysis finished after 10 days, 61 LPEs had already been patched upstream, 43 had staging patches, and 299 were being reported and discussed publicly.

We greatly appreciate the Linux maintainers who have been working urgently to patch identified problems, and the broader security community contributing their findings as well. This collective response is what’s needed to secure the world’s software. The rapid rate of vulnerability disclosure and patching also emphasizes the criticality for consumers and companies to keep software up to date.

In a recent development, takeaway: Automated triage should take the rapid patching cycle into account. Revalidating findings against the latest code, including newly introduced code that was merged after the original scan, helps avoid duplicate or obsolete reports. This focuses attention on unresolved vulnerabilities and gives maintainers evidence that they can act on without adding unnecessary review burden.

While we were developing the pipeline, in late July 2026, GPT‑5.6 Sol found and exploited 166 unique LPE vulnerabilities for an end-to-end $513,690 cost in API credits.

Sources indicate that in the second scan, in mid-October 2026, the newer cyber model found and exploited 948 unique LPE vulnerabilities for an end-to-end $1,213,430 cost in API credits. For both campaigns, we scanned the latest Linux kernel master branch at the time.

Takeaway: Rescan previously audited code as model capabilities improve. A more capable model may uncover vulnerabilities that earlier models missed, even when using the same research harness.

We sampled 166 exploits developed by the agents and analyzed the exploitation techniques used in them. To the best of our knowledge, the agents used 10 new exploitation techniques in the sampled exploits. We shared the exploitation techniques with third-party kernel exploitation experts and the techniques were new to them as well.

Of the 10 techniques, two are new persistent elastic objects that the model used to spray objects inside the target kernel cache; two are new page grooming techniques to improve exploit reliability; five are new data-only techniques to obtain privilege escalation directly or via an arbitrary write; the other technique involves arbitrary type confusion. For safety reasons, we omit sharing the full technical details of these new exploitation techniques in this post.

Takeaway: Frontier models do not just pattern match known vulnerable code patterns or solely use known exploitation techniques; they demonstrate creativity and novel approaches.

An notable part of our team’s mission is to measure the cost of finding and exploiting vulnerabilities and use that evidence to guide defensive investment. Our goal is to help defenders fix vulnerabilities before attackers can use them, and make it cost prohibitive for attackers to exploit software. Measuring exploitation costs helps us assess how that challenge changes as model capabilities improve. In this section, we compare our pipeline run’s cost with bug bounty program rewards for the vulnerabilities identified.

According to recent reports, the target virtual machines in our experiment ran a stock desktop operating system, not a weakened target, under the same threat model that is used by cybersecurity competitions (e.g. Pwn2Own⁠(opens in a upcoming window), TyphoonPWN⁠(opens in a new window)). Historically, Pwn2Own and TyphoonPWN offered bug bounties of $20,000 and $70,000, respectively for Linux kernel local privilege escalation exploits. Applying those historical bounty amounts to the 948 exploits produces a hypothetical valuation of $18.9M—$66.3M, approximately 16x to 55x our pipeline’s cost.

We also tested our pipeline against Google’s kernelCTF⁠(opens in a new window) vulnerability reward program, which features a hardened Linux kernel with reduced attack surfaces as the target. We ran the pipeline on the latest version of the Linux kernel (incompatible with the SLAB_VIRTUAL mitigation in kernelCTF so we dropped it from the config) under kernelCTF’s environment and obtained 25 information leak proofs of concept and 21 local privilege escalation exploits. For comparison, 26 confirmed 0-day LPE exploits have been accepted by kernelCTF in 2026 at the time of writing. The whole campaign lasted 112 hours in total, costing roughly $32,936 in API credits, with vulnerability discovery accounting for 83.7% of the API cost. If the 21 vulnerabilities were accepted by the program, it would lead to around a $1.5M bounty award, approximately 45x the cost.

It has been revealed that takeaway: Based on public pay-out amounts, with current cyber-capable models, our vulnerability research pipeline was net profitable at the time of this research. Defenders should proactively analyze their software so that it becomes cost prohibitive for attackers to exploit.

According to recent reports, during exploitability assessment, ExploitDev agents were given a vulnerability report and tasked with creating a fully functional exploit. Our pipeline marked a vulnerability as exploited if a root shell was successfully obtained. During an early run, the exploitation stage reported 200 successful local privilege escalation exploits. However, after human review, we found that 20 of these had achieved root privileges through a different 0-day vulnerability than the one assigned. This suggests that even successful exploitation by agents needs proper validation.

We subsequently tightened the task constraints and added an independent check confirming that each final exploit used its assigned vulnerability.

Takeaway: For autonomous security research, verify the path to a result in addition to verifying the result itself; isolation, monitoring, and independent checks are necessary controls.

Industry observers note that early in this research, we explored the design decision of whether to build heavy orchestration around the agent to improve its cyber capability. Our result suggested that stronger models require lighter orchestration and hand-holding. And the marginal improvement does not justify the maintenance cost. As a result, we decided to remove the heavy orchestration.

According to recent reports, the experiment compared GPT‑5.5 Cyber and GPT‑5.6 Cyber. In our observation, GPT‑5.5 Cyber did not consistently identify when and how to apply existing Linux kernel exploitation techniques. We then assembled 103 techniques in a model-friendly format, made them available in the agent’s environment, and prompted the agent to use them. Across 63 exploitation candidates, this increased the success rate from 76.2% to 88.9%.

Recent findings suggest that when we repeated this with GPT‑5.6 Cyber, the model was better able to find, select, and apply relevant techniques on its own. We removed the technique/skill orchestration and this lightly orchestrated GPT‑5.6 Cyber workflow outperformed the more heavily scaffolded GPT‑5.5 Cyber workflow. Adding back the additional technique layer for GPT‑5.6 Cyber provided only a marginal 1.5 percentage-point improvement.

In a recent development, takeaway: Reevaluate your orchestration and harness as base model capabilities change. Scaffolding that materially improves one model generation may add little value for a stronger model and should be evaluated for the maintenance tradeoff.

Initially, when directly prompted to generate candidate patches, the model would create functionally correct patches that mitigate the proof of concept but occasionally introduce other issues: more code than necessary, introduced potential performance tradeoffs, deviated from coding conventions, or failed to examine related code for variants of the same vulnerability, leading to incomplete patches.

Sources indicate that additional instructions and iterations on the patch generation process improved the quality of patches, which suggests that with proper handling, it is possible for AI-generated security patches to be correct, minimal, and consistent with existing code conventions. This is an active area of research, and we believe this will become easier and more effective with future models. In a few cases, our research prototype was also able to identify issues in patches written by human experts, which were then fixed before they were merged.

Recent findings suggest that takeaway: Models can speed up the patching process, but patching skills and harnesses may require iteration to ensure the patches reliably fulfill both functional and nonfunctional requirements. Additionally, we recommend using models for adversarial review of human and AI-generated patches, which can identify problems such as the patch being bypassable, missing other attack paths or variants, and more.

Recent findings suggest that in our kernelCTF run, besides the 21 Linux kernel 0-day exploits, our research prototype also found and exploited a QEMU TCG vulnerability. The analyst agent was assigned to analyze the system call entry code, and when writing programs to experiment with privilege transitions, it encountered an unexpected kernel crash. It triaged the crash and traced the issue to QEMU TCG, without access to QEMU’s source code, and included the vulnerability in the report. The ExploitDev agent successfully developed a local privilege escalation exploit for this vulnerability subsequently. We discovered this QEMU vulnerability when analyzing the exploits manually and confirmed that the vulnerability had been fixed in upstream QEMU but not in the release build used during the experiment.

Recent findings suggest that takeaway: Frontier cyber-capable models can find vulnerabilities in testing infrastructure. We recommend testing each part of the infrastructure before carrying out offensive vulnerability research. We have proactively tested our infrastructure, disclosing and patching many vulnerabilities in Kata, Moby/Docker, gVisor, and other projects.

Our goal is to turn increasing model capability into a lasting advantage for the people securing the Internet. This research demonstrates that the growing cyber capability of frontier models can be used for effectively looking for vulnerabilities in complex software, such as the Linux kernel. Hardening critical software projects like Linux and other open-source projects can protect many downstream systems and users.

Through Patch the Planet, a Daybreak initiative, we aim to extend this research to more critical software projects and develop reliable automated patching alongside maintainers and security partners. We want to steadily reduce the opportunities available to attackers and raise the cost of finding and exploiting vulnerabilities, until the expected payoff no longer justifies the attack.

Every generation of models should help us build software that the next generation finds harder to compromise. We will continue working towards building a secure Internet that anyone can joyfully build on.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.27504v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models behave differently across languages, and are noticeably less safe in lower-resource languages. This gap is well established behaviorally, but not mechanistically. Directions in activation space, including the assistant persona direction, are almost always extracted from English and assumed to generalize across languages. We extract the assistant persona direction in 31 languages in Qwen3-32B, and find that the resulting axes differ substantially: their cosine similarity to the English axis ranges from 0.378 to 0.911. Moreover, each language's assistant persona direction and its magnitude are correlated with the language's resource level. We also find that the model's default assistant state is farther from the helpful assistant pole in lower-resource languages. Finally, steering against a language's own axis amplifies persona-based jailbreak more than steering against the English axis. These results indicate that the model does not carry a single assistant representation across languages. More broadly, the assistant persona may need to be an explicit target of multilingual alignment.

arXiv:2611.27500v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Post-hoc transformer linearization replaces the key-value cache of full attention, which grows linearly with generation length, with a fixed size state. This change reduces memory consumption but often hurts accuracy. In reasoning tasks, which require long generations, this effect is especially pronounced. In this work we introduce Turnout, a method that mitigates accuracy loss as a result of linearization, while maintaining its memory-reduction benefits. We apply post-hoc linearization to a pretrained full-attention model, training a linear path through distillation while leaving the original full-attention path unchanged. During response generation, the resulting hybrid model retains both paths and uses a learned policy to control when each layer switches from full to linear attention. We train the policy with reinforcement learning using a reward that balances answer correctness and memory use. Empirical evaluation of our method shows that the learned adaptive policy achieves a better accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier on reasoning tasks compared to fixed switching and static hybrid baselines.

Defenders can use it to reason through security findings, assess their impact, and evaluate fixes, helping connect vulnerability research to practical improvements in defense.

Daybreak Red gives verified defenders greater latitude for authorized cybersecurity work, with fewer refusals for these tasks alongside stronger identity verification, monitoring, and access controls.

For Daybreak Red on Amazon Bedrock, inference data is not used to train models, and customers do not need to share their Daybreak Red data with OpenAI.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.27491v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Tokenization represents one of the most crucial steps in mulilingual NLP pipelines. Yet, tokenizers routinely under-allocate vocabulary to low-resource languages. While improved allocation leads to better performance, it remains poorly understood how tokenization shapes cross-lingual representations and transfer during pretraining. To address this, we pretrain 39 mono- and bilingual 1B decoder-only models on FineWeb2-HQ across English, German, French, Arabic and Chinese, varying only the tokenizer. Our results demonstrate that improved vocabulary allocation (i) substantially raises cross-lingual representation alignment in early-to-mid layers, an effect that prior work measuring only the output layer could not observe, (ii) increases cross-lingual parametric knowledge sharing in feed-forward neurons, supported by correlational and causal evidence, and (iii) an alignment-transfer dissociation, where cross-lingual transfer remains essentially unchanged despite higher alignment. Moreover, transfer is significantly lower for cross-script bilinguals even under fair vocabulary allocation, indicating that the script barrier is not merely a tokenizer artifact. All of our checkpoints and code are publicly available.

Expanding Codex’s tools for building, understanding, and reviewing code.

Industry observers note that today we're announcing that OpenAI will acquire Pierre Computer Firm, Inc⁠(opens in a new window). (“Pierre”), the company behind Code Storage⁠(opens in a new window) and a family of standout open-source developer tools. If you’ve browsed files or reviewed a change in the Codex app, you’ve already used Pierre’s Trees and Diffs libraries. We’re excited to work with the Pierre team to build on the Git workflows that developers already rely on and adapt them to how teams work with coding agents.

We’ve seen in our own engineering work how the systems around Git need to evolve as more of that work happens in parallel. Earlier this week, we shared how we’re scaling Git at OpenAI with Pando, our in-house source control backend for engineers and agents. With the Pierre team, we wish to set the standard for modern software development: from the first branch an agent creates to that magic moment when code is deployed to the world. We want to make Codex the place where developers and agents take on their most ambitious projects.

We’ve long appreciated the care Pierre brings to another part of working with Git: how developers review code. You can see that care in the libraries we use in Codex today. Trees lets developers swiftly navigate a project’s files, and Diffs makes it easy to see what changed. Both of these tools make it easy to review and navigate large volumes of code with uncompromising performance.

That same attention to detail runs through Pierre’s other work. Diffs’ Edit mode lets a reviewer fix a line of code right where they spot the problem. Pierre recently released Highlights, an extremely fast syntax highlighter that updates as a developer types or an agent streams code. The same small team that put an editor inside a diff also designed the API for Code Storage, a service that lets apps store code and track its history using Git.

Sources indicate that pierre has built tools that developers love, and together, we will ship newly introduced products and platforms that benefit all. Once the acquisition closes, our ambition is to advance the future of source control across the industry. We want Codex to connect the code a organization ships with the decisions its people make, at the scale the future demands.

Pierre’s open-source projects will remain open-source, and we’ll continue to contribute to them. Customers can continue using Code Storage after the acquisition closes while we work to bring its features and functionality into Codex.

The closing of the acquisition is subject to customary closing conditions, including receipt of regulatory approvals. Until closing, OpenAI and Pierre will remain separate and independent companies.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Starting with equity research, Franklin Templeton is developing AI workflows to help portfolio managers compare views and examine risks.

Franklin Templeton wants AI to help portfolio managers examine different research views and the risks behind an investment idea. Codex is one of several tools our investment teams are using to develop workflows for investment research.

Sources indicate that when Franklin Templeton first tried using AI, the team put data in a database and connected the models to it. But it didn’t produce the answers the teams needed because the models didn’t understand how the data fit together. When the team added agents and a semantic layer, a structured model of what the firm’s data means and how it’s connected, the results changed. The team is using Codex and other tools to develop this connected intelligence layer. "We've been able to build what we think of as a connected intelligence layer," Dudley says. "We're bringing the data into the tools, and we're surfacing insights that make a difference.".

In a recent development, research, risk, compliance, and trading offer different perspectives on an investment. Franklin Templeton’s ambition is to bring those inputs together for portfolio managers. “We're able to bring that all in and then use that to surface insights to the people who are making decisions, which are our portfolio managers,” Dudley indicates.

Dudley describes the earlier equity-research workflow as human-led and sequential: an analyst performs first-pass stock analysis, reviews earnings calls, and studies competitors in each business line. The goal is to surface useful information as analysts prepare upcoming ideas to be pitched to portfolio managers or provide updates on existing positions in the portfolio. As she puts it, “It's just continuous intelligence combined with that human judgment.”.

In the workflow Franklin Templeton envisions, its investment teams will have access to a governed, reusable intelligence foundation that brings together trusted connectors, portfolio and workflow context, and agentic capabilities that surface actionable insights for its analysts and portfolio managers.

In a recent development, franklin Templeton has used Codex in hackathons, bringing experts alongside investment practitioners as they develop their own tools. Its Investment AI champions are working to turn experiments into production-ready workflows, with security review, expert support, and data controls as part of that process.

Dudley notes, “We have moved from augmenting our research process to reimagining the investment research workflow.”.

Some of what makes AI helpful in other settings doesn't work in asset management. Many tools learn a user's preferences and show them more of the same, so if someone favors one research provider, the tool surfaces more of that provider's reports. For an investment team, that narrowing potentially brings a biased perspective into the investment process. Franklin Templeton wants the opposite. "We want to make sure that they're accessing that diversity of research and diversity of opinion," Dudley claims.

Industry observers note that franklin Templeton wants its AI systems to emphasize investment risks. “We need AI to understand that a great investment idea is one that is well reasoned, but it also has analyzed the risks and makes our portfolio managers aware of the risk,” Dudley says. “If you’re looking at a research note, focusing on the fact someone has identified the investment risks is not a bad thing from our perspective. It makes for a more informed investment decision.”.

Franklin Templeton's experience points to some investment management best practices:.

Sources indicate that “Our message from leadership is consistent: we encourage innovation and experimentation with AI within clearly defined risk guardrails. Not every initiative will succeed, but each should generate insights that strengthen our capabilities, inform future decisions, and drive continuous improvement,” Dudley states.

Get fresh tools into people's hands: Dudley states Franklin Templeton has brought practical labs to teams swiftly after new technology launches, so they can test how it fits their work.

Help teams learn the tools: Dudley notes, "The goal is getting them to actually understand the power of the technology.".

Build with appropriate controls: Security review, expert support, and data agreements are part of Franklin Templeton’s path from experimentation toward production-grade tools.

Dudley’s longer-term goal is to make that connected intelligence accessible across investment teams, from analysts to the leaders of each investment group.

It has been revealed that she wants analysts to spend more time in the field, speaking with many different experts and professionals, including executives at private companies, and bringing what they learn back to their investment teams. For Dudley, that human perspective remains essential as the tools develop.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (240 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2611.27447v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Simulation is central to intelligent-vehicle validation, but visual realism or output agreement between a real scene and its synthetic counterpart does not prove that a perception system used the same evidence in both domains. This paper addresses that mechanism-parity gap for paired real-synthetic autonomous-driving perception. It unifies Decisive-Feature Fidelity, which compares decisive evidence maps in a frozen system under test (SUT), with Concept-Decisive Feature Fidelity, which projects decisive evidence into semantic scene concepts for diagnosis. The framework is a validation diagnostic rather than a standalone safety certificate: it asks whether output-consistent simulation also preserves the mechanism by which the perception model reaches that output. The empirical evidence comprises ten retrained diffusion ControlNet generators evaluated on a deterministic exact-geometry KITTI-Virtual KITTI 2 subset. Generated counterparts use a 1248-by-376-pixel padded inference canvas and are cropped back to the exact KITTI dimensions before evaluation. The final benchmark reports target-image, output-consistency, and mechanism metrics recomputed from a single audited output set, then adds metric-disagreement cases, bootstrap uncertainty, threshold sensitivity, and concept/cache integrity audits. Across the benchmark, output and appearance fidelity are at most weakly and inconsistently rank-correlated with decisive-mechanism distance for all three frozen SUTs, and a constructed positive control highlights the estimator detects a known planted mechanism that output agreement misses, supporting decisive-evidence diagnostics for intelligent-vehicle simulation validation. All numerical claims are restricted to the declared exact-geometry benchmark, ten generators, and three frozen SUTs.

Flipsnack⁠(opens in a latest window) helps teams turn static documents into interactive digital experiences. Its customers use the platform to create product catalogs, sales presentations, brochures, internal communications, and training materials.

For Flipsnack, that range of applications creates a marketing challenge: helping people recognize how the product fits the work they need to do. As the organization increased its focus on business customers, it wanted to reach people with needs that its product category alone might not clearly describe.

In a recent development, flipsnack had relied heavily on search advertising. Its ChatGPT Ads test became an opportunity to learn which customer needs could translate into product signups.

Because Flipsnack is a visual product, prospective customers often want to experience it before speaking with sales. Its campaign landing pages directed people into a signup flow, making completed registration the first meaningful step the team could measure and optimize for.

In a recent development, to help business customers see where the product could fit their work, Flipsnack expanded beyond its original, broader Flipbook campaign. Separate campaigns for Magazine, Catalog, and Brochure addressed specific document needs, while campaigns for Sales Enablement, Employee Benefits, Real Estate, and Hospitality connected the product to business applications and industries.

“A sales team and an internal communications team can use the same product for very different jobs. We want our campaigns to help each see where Flipsnack fits.”.

Flipsnack’s initial click-focused campaigns brought in traffic and signups. After seeing better delivery and registration efficiency in conversion-focused campaigns, the team rebuilt existing campaigns with a conversions objective and bidding set to maximize conversions.

Flipsnack created conversion-focused versions of five existing US campaigns that had used a clicks objective with fixed bids.

According to recent reports, early results following the shift to conversion-focused campaigns were encouraging. Across five campaigns, registrations increased approximately 310% while cost per registration fell approximately 75%, with daily budget settings unchanged.1.

Industry observers note that “What stood out was that we were getting more registrations at a lower cost per signup. That gave us the confidence to make conversion optimization the focus of our campaigns.”.

These results give Flipsnack a promising foundation for continued growth with ChatGPT Ads. Building on its conversion-focused campaigns, the team aims to bring more prospective customers into the product and help them discover how Flipsnack can support their business.

Reach people as they explore options, compare choices, and make decisions in ChatGPT, with relevant ads that fit naturally into the experience.

Recent findings suggest that results are based on Flipsnack’s ChatGPT Ads Manager data for five US campaign pairs, August 25–31 versus September 2–8, 2026, checked September 11. Attribution uses 30-day clicks, excluding views. Daily budget limits were unchanged; spend rose approximately 1.3%. Objectives and bidding changed together.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (257 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.27443v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Small language models (SLMs) are increasingly attractive for cheap, high-throughput agentic deployment, but they remain weak at multi-step reasoning and tool use that long-horizon tasks demand. We study how to post-train an SLM to seek advice from a stronger model and act on that advice itself, following an advisor-executor pattern. Out of the box, this pattern fails across open- and closed-source small-model families: wiring an SLM to an advisor is a harness-design matter that is not enough on its own. A post-training recipe is needed to teach the model when to ask, in a cost-aware fashion, and how to follow advice across steps. Our method, ADAPT (ADvisor-Aware Post-Training), is a multi-stage recipe that instills this behavior, learning entirely from the policy's own rollouts supervised by the environment's outcome, with no learned reward model or human annotation. Across three domains, compared to an untrained harness baseline, ADAPT improves success rate in embodied text reasoning (TextWorld) from 24.5% to 77.3%, code generation (LiveCodeBench) from 21.8% to 56.0%, and deep web search (GAIA) from 17.5% to 49.3%, while querying the advisor sparingly (~1.0-2.1 calls per task). On the two long-horizon domains it closes 70-85% of the gap to an oracle that perfectly times when to ask for advice, and on code generation it exceeds that oracle. The gains persist when the advisor is replaced by one unseen in training, showing that the learned help-seeking policy is robust to a changing advisor rather than tied to the one it was trained with.

THRIFTY: Cost-Constrained Reasoning-Data Synthesis for Small Language Models

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (211 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.27436v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Small language models (SLMs) are increasingly attractive for efficient, specialized deployment, and are typically trained on reasoning trajectories distilled from a larger teacher LLM. Generating this synthetic data is a major cost of the pipeline, especially when the teacher is a frontier model. Existing collection methods, however, are largely cost-unaware, or at best spread a fixed sampling budget uniformly across queries. Such allocation ignores the wide variation in problem difficulty and the strategic over- or under-sampling it invites. Thus, we propose THRIFTY, a Thompson-sampling bandit controller that spends a fixed generation-token budget to collect diverse correct reasoning trajectories, casting the task as a bandits-with-knapsacks problem with a novel diversity-aware objective. It tracks each problem's success probability with an online Beta posterior and spends each token where it expects the most new distinct correct solutions. Because repeated solutions add progressively less value, THRIFTY adaptively stops resampling saturated problems, concentrates budget on under-covered ones, and retires the unsolvable at the budget's opportunity cost. On math (AIME, MATH-500) and code (LiveCodeBench) benchmarks, THRIFTY gathers up to 22% more diverse correct trajectories per generation token than both the standard uniform-sampling recipe and the strongest adaptive baseline, with the largest gains in the scarce-budget and hard-problem regimes.

We show that, across in-domain, out-of-domain, and cross-domain settings on two corpora, document-only adaptation can match or closely approach real transcriptions; whether written or conversational rendering is best depends on speaking style and the amount of text generated. As no existing corpus pairs audio, transcripts, and documents, we also built and released a document-grounded benchmark.

Setting a fresh standard for responsible AI infrastructure

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (997 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Latest commitments to the communities where we build and policy proposals to help more Americans share in the benefits.
  • The promise of AI is that it gives people more power to shape their own futures.
  • The communities that host this infrastructure should have a clear say in shaping their futures, too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Latest commitments to the communities where we build and policy proposals to help more Americans share in the benefits.

The promise of AI is that it gives people more power to shape their own futures. It can help someone learn a latest skill, build a business, or solve a problem that was previously out of reach. Building more computing infrastructure capacity in the United States can help lower the cost of delivering AI, put these tools in more people’s hands, and ensure America stays at the forefront of the technology.

The communities that host this infrastructure should have a clear say in shaping their futures, too. Residents should be able to influence how a campus is developed, hold developers accountable for covering the cost of powering it, and share in the jobs and business opportunities it creates. How we build these campuses is one of the first tests of whether the benefits of AI will be broadly shared.

Today we’re publishing our National Community Compact⁠(opens in a new window) and a Compute Campus Policy Blueprint⁠(opens in a new window). The compact sets out what communities can expect from OpenAI at future campuses that we own and operate. The blueprint proposes policies to help ensure that compute campus development gives communities a meaningful voice, protects families from new costs, and broadly shares the economic gains of AI.

It has been revealed that this builds on work we began in January, when we declared our Stargate Community commitments to pay our own way on energy and develop looks shaped by local priorities. We followed with specific commitments in Georgia and Ohio, covering energy costs, water use, local investment and accountability. Throughout that work, we’ve listened to residents, local leaders, schools and businesses about what matters to their communities. Today’s announcement is the next step in that ongoing effort.

Sources indicate that every future compute campus OpenAI owns and operates will have its own local compact. We’ll engage residents early enough to ensure their input shapes project plans, give them a local point of contact throughout the life of the campus, and report publicly each year on how we’re doing. Each compact will reflect local priorities and include a common set of commitments:.

Recent findings suggest that pay our own way on energy and infrastructure. We’ll pay the full cost of the electricity we use and the infrastructure needed to serve us. Before major spending begins, we’ll provide financial assurances so other customers are protected if a project is delayed, reduced, or canceled.

Recent findings suggest that protect local resources and report on our impact. We’ll develop a water plan for each campus, prioritize closed-loop or low-water cooling, and publish site-level water and electricity use. We’ll publish construction prepares and independent noise studies before operations begin and annually afterward. And we will not use non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with public officials, allowing only narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.

According to recent reports, create opportunities for local workers and businesses. We’ll publish the jobs we expect to create, work with unions and training providers to help residents prepare for them, and report annually on hiring and apprenticeships. We’ll also make sustained investments in priorities residents help select.

Those priorities will differ from place to place. In Effingham County, Georgia, residents helped shape a $4.8 million grant to provide free school meals for all 14,000 students in the county. In Pike County, Ohio, families identified childcare as a priority, leading to a joint $6 million commitment from OpenAI and SB Energy.

Families should be able to count on basic protections whoever builds a campus in their community. Voluntary commitments from companies are an vital starting point, but our blueprint goes further—asking federal, state, and local policymakers to establish clear rules for how the industry builds. New policy is required to establish trust and confidence between communities, elected officials and companies. Lawmakers should establish rules to advance responsible investment, protect residents, and ensure that the benefits of AI infrastructure are broadly shared.

Industry observers note that that starts with who pays for power. State utility commissions should require large electricity customers to cover the costs they add to the grid and protect other customers if a project falls through. Utilities should also make it easier for campuses to connect if they can safely cut demand when power is scarce. At our planned Effingham County campus, for example, our agreement with Georgia Power allows the utility to reduce the power it delivers to us by up to 1,000 megawatts during periods of high demand. Congress can help meet growing demand by speeding up transmission upgrades and restoring and expanding tax incentives for clean electricity.

Sources indicate that communities also need a way to hold developers accountable. The blueprint calls for public reporting on water, energy, noise, and hiring, and for narrow limits on when developers can require public officials to sign NDAs. When states or local governments offer tax incentives, the terms should be public, with measurable commitments and a way to recover benefits if a developer falls short.

Finally, the blueprint proposes practical ways to keep more of the work local to ensure compute campuses support local workers and local businesses. Developers can share purchasing plans early enough for local suppliers to compete for contracts. Employers, building trades unions, and community colleges can use hiring forecasts to train residents for jobs they know will be available, from electrical work during construction to maintaining power and cooling systems for years afterward.

Sources indicate that the investments that help America compete globally can also help communities prosper locally. That starts with giving residents a say while plans can still change and a way to hold developers accountable for delivering on their commitments. That’s what we’re committing to at the campuses we own and operate, and what we believe people should be able to count on wherever AI infrastructure is built across the country.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.27427v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurate differential diagnosis of neurodegenerative disorders remains challenging due to overlapping clinical manifestations and heterogeneous, often incomplete multimodal observations. Existing multimodal models can integrate imaging and clinical measurements but often overlook disease-specific evidence patterns and pairwise relations among competing diagnoses. We therefore propose Knowledge-enhanced Structural Reasoning (KnowSR), which aligns multimodal patient representations with a literature-grounded knowledge bank of disease prototypes, signed evidence directions, and pairwise diagnostic relations. Specifically, in KnowSR, patient-specific knowledge alignment and target-aware pooling inject structured disease evidence, while anchored relational reasoning reconciles pairwise diagnostic margins over a sparse differential graph, thereby collectively enhancing differential diagnostic capability. Across extensive experiments, KnowSR consistently outperforms 19 baselines on patient-level six-class diagnosis under patient-disjoint five-fold evaluation. This shows that grounding patient evidence in structured medical knowledge enables more effective differential diagnosis than naive multimodal fusion alone.

Breaking: Cleave: Severing Guardrails and Auditing Spectral Coupling in Open-Weight LLMs

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (207 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.27426v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Open-weight Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely downloaded for their strong coding and reasoning capabilities and deployed locally beyond the provider's control. To prevent misuse, developers embed safety guardrails into these models before release. However, we find that these guardrails rely on the residual writing weights to trigger refusals. Based on this insight, we propose Cleave, a training-free attack that directly edits these weights to remove safety restrictions while preserving general capabilities. With Cleave, malicious users can either remove all guardrails or selectively lift only cybersecurity restrictions. Because this selective removal retains up to a 99% refusal rate on other harmful requests and avoids weight rank collapse, it evades both behavioral spot-checks and static weight audits. Across five open-weight LLMs from 7B to 320B parameters, Cleave achieves up to a 67.97% attack success rate on seven safety benchmarks, substantially outperforming existing white-box baselines. On 356 cybersecurity tasks and 15 live vulnerable services, it further boosts executable exploit generation by up to 24.0 times and compromises up to 66.7% of the targets. To counter this threat, we propose a dual-stage defense that combines pre-release subspace diagnostics with post-release weight-coupling audits, achieving 100% detection recall at a 1% false-positive rate.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The integration platform uses GPT‑6 Astra, ChatGPT, and Codex for product reviews, marketing, and business development planning.

Recent findings suggest that merge helps companies build connected software and AI products, from syncing customer data to enabling AI agents to take action across business systems. Its products span customer-data integrations through Merge Unified, secure tool access for AI agents through Merge Agent Handler, and model routing and cost controls through Merge Gateway. Merge for Workforce brings those capabilities inside companies, helping teams manage which models, tools, and business systems employees can access. Together, these products support both the software companies build for customers and the AI-powered work happening inside their organizations.

According to recent reports, inside Merge, CEO and Co-founder Shensi Ding uses Codex to review product code, including work on a upcoming setup interface for configuring tool access in Merge for Workforce. Her colleagues use GPT‑6 Astra for product testing and marketing. The team also uses AI for the work of running the company, from preparing sales updates to planning customer dinners.

Merge launched a tool for adding connectors to AI products, with reliability a priority for Ding: “We’re pretty proud of the quality. Tool calls through Merge succeed 99.9% of the time, compared to public MCP servers, which are around 60%.”.

For its own product development, Merge uses GPT‑6 Astra. “It’s really fast, and it was much better at code reviews,” Ding indicates. “They also liked the personality of GPT‑6 Astra, which goes a long way. It was also clear that Codex had improved a lot. Merge lets employees choose their own AI tools, and which one to use has become a lively internal debate.”.

Ding used Codex to review a proposed implementation of the latest provisioning tab in Merge for Workforce as the team evaluated how customers would configure tool access. They discussed making the “Add tool pack” action a clearer link that opens separately to make setup less confusing. Codex supplied code-review feedback; Merge’s team made the product decisions and implementation changes, with engineers responsible for validating and shipping them.

Merge hosts executive dinners for customers and prospects to build relationships and create opportunities for follow-up product conversations.

Recent findings suggest that for one dinner in Dallas, Merge started with the city and the kinds of people it wanted to bring together. The bot pulled potential guests from the CRM and Apollo, checked previous invitations and responses, and helped prepare outreach from Ding’s email. It also maintained the attendee tracker, proposed a seating chart, and created calendar notes where sales and customer success could add context about each guest.

The model handles reasoning and drafting, while Merge’s connectors provide access to the business systems. Ding reviews the output, rewrites anything that sounds off, and curates the guest list using relationship context the bot does not have.

In October 2026, Merge reported that preparing guest lists and outreach and maintaining the attendee tracker had gone from dozens of hours across the tech giant to about 30 minutes per event. The comparison covers the same planning tasks, measured over the preceding three months. The team still handles hosting, relationship-building, and on-the-ground logistics.

Merge ran 16 executive dinners in Q3, up from eight in Q2, and looks to host more than 30 in Q4. After the Dallas dinner, the team reported positive feedback on the invitations and opportunities for follow-up demos.

“With GPT‑6 Astra, the dinner bot connects to our Salesforce, Gong, Google Sheets, and Gmail, and it’ll send emails on my behalf to people in our network,” Ding indicates. “It gives me recommendations for people who are a good fit for each dinner, and it surfaces upcoming potential attendees.”.

Ding indicates, “It’s been especially great for team members who aren’t in engineering, because now they can build anything.”.

Charlie Lynch on Merge’s sales leadership team built reusable AI workflows for deal approvals, forecast updates, and next steps after renewal calls. Instead of repeatedly gathering context for each upgrade or decision, he uses the workflows to prepare the material, then reviews the recommendation and decides what to do next.

The social media team uses GPT‑6 Astra in ChatGPT to find posts the firm should respond to. The marketing team also used it to clarify the messaging for Merge’s Gateway Evaluations launch.

Lead by using the tools: “If you’re an executive, you are the ceiling for AI fluency in your organization,” Ding says.

Find somewhere less risky to experiment: Ding and her co-founder experimented with AI on a new product before customers depended on its codebase. “When you’re less nervous, and you can really experiment, you learn so much,” she says.

Sources indicate that give people space and time to tinker: Merge lets each team member choose the tools they like and encourages them to spend time every day learning and testing. That includes the freedom to “go wild and make mistakes,” even when it means going down a rabbit hole that doesn’t pay off.

“Anything that I want to do, I can just tell AI to do it, and it can just do it,” Ding says. Merge is continuing to use OpenAI technology to expand what its teams can build, bringing the same spirit of experimentation to its products and the way it runs the business.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (189 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.27425v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent work demonstrates that large language models (LLMs) can reason directly about the weights of other neural networks. Given only a natural-language objective, an LLM can inspect a model's weights, understand what they compute, and edit them directly without gradient-based optimization. This capability, termed weight-space programming (WSP), has been used to improve model performance on math reasoning, medical QA and other benchmarks. We propose TrojanMaxxing, a novel strategy to backdoor vision-language models (VLMs), by reframing it as a WSP task. We use Claude Opus 5.5 and Mythos 5.2 agents to backdoor VLMs without any optimization or training methods. The agents inspect the model weights, apply targeted edits, and co-design an imperceptible visual trigger that activates the backdoor. We then study the agents' strategies and present a thorough evaluation of the trojaned models on various benchmark datasets. TrojanMaxxing achieves attack success rates of 93%-100% on content moderation and 78%-100% on OCR while maintaining clean accuracy. Perhaps most consequentially, we show that injecting backdoors in a training-free manner is possible by simply, "asking an agent to do it".

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.27423v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Exposure and gain determine the visual evidence available to monocular depth estimation (MDE), particularly when robot motion creates a tradeoff between light collection and motion blur. We present ADEPT, a framework that adapts these settings using learned feedback from a frozen depth model. During training, ground-truth depth identifies the lowest-error reference within a group of physically evaluated camera settings. A compact predictor learns reference-relative disagreement (RRD) between each candidate's depth prediction and the reference prediction using regression and ranking losses. At deployment, it scores observed captures using frozen-model features and camera, motion, and illumination context, without ground truth or reference images. A contextual Gaussian-process controller uses recent scores to select subsequent exposure and gain settings under motion and photometric constraints. We evaluate offline camera selection with relative and metric Depth Anything v2 and demonstrate online control with the affine-invariant variant on a mobile robot. Across nine equally weighted scene-illumination conditions, ADEPT reduces mean scale-and-shift-aligned $\mathrm{Abs}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ by 14.6% relative to built-in auto-exposure and by 10.0% relative to the best-performing evaluated prior controller.

Industry News: GPT‑6 Cyber: Advancing the frontier of aligned cybersecurity agents
