arXiv:2611.27264v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) still struggle with fine-grained understanding of high-resolution images: attention heads vary in their reliability for grounding target entities and their attributes, while localized details are often disconnected from the broader scene context. We propose EAGLE (Entity-Aware Grounding with Layered Evidence for High-Resolution Image Understanding), a plug-in framework that jointly selects grounding signals and organizes hierarchical visual evidence. EAGLE employs a fine-grained dataset to screen visually-grounded attention heads, followed by entity-aware grounding to extract target-specific regions. It then integrates hierarchical evidence construction and question-guided routing to select optimal view combinations, feeding them into the frozen MLLM to enhance fine-grained visual understanding. Experiments with Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3-8B demonstrate that EAGLE consistently improves performance across both backbones and achieves SOTA results on V*, HRBench-4K, and HRBench-8K compared with existing methods using the same backbone.

  • For Harjot Gill, co-founder and CEO of CodeRabbit⁠(opens in a upcoming window), trusting and validating agentic code is becoming the place where teams bring judgment to a growing volume of AI-generated work.
  • It has been revealed that codeRabbit built an AI-powered governance and control platform designed to validate and trust AI-generated code.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CodeRabbit uses OpenAI models to govern and trust AI-generated code and Codex to ship 20 times more software with the same engineering team.

For Harjot Gill, co-founder and CEO of CodeRabbit⁠(opens in a upcoming window), trusting and validating agentic code is becoming the place where teams bring judgment to a growing volume of AI-generated work. “The first bottleneck that every firm hits as soon as you adopt coding agents is code reviews,” Harjot states.

It has been revealed that codeRabbit built an AI-powered governance and control platform designed to validate and trust AI-generated code. Used by over 20,000 organizations and 150,000+ open-source projects, CodeRabbit helps teams understand, review, and secure code produced by AI agents and decide what is ready to ship.

According to CodeRabbit, better price-performance from OpenAI helps it add more AI agents to its reviews and pass the benefits to customers, and Codex⁠ helps it ship 20 times more software with the same engineering team. The organization also uses Daybreak⁠ to both secure its own stack and its customers’ code. Its latest offering, CodeRabbit Secure, uses Daybreak with Codex models to find and fix vulnerabilities using its security-focused agents.

Recent findings suggest that codeRabbit built its first product with GPT‑3.5 Turbo. Harjot indicates the arrival of GPT‑4 made the product effective at reviewing code. The company went on to adopt OpenAI o1 and OpenAI o3 early. Because code reviews run asynchronously in the cloud, CodeRabbit could use models that took longer to reason through a problem in exchange for more capable analysis.

It has been revealed that the team evaluates latest models against its own benchmark of known complications. At the time of the interview, Harjot estimated that GPT‑6 Astra⁠ caught 50% of the issues in that dataset, putting it at the top compared to other models in that benchmark.

The benchmark continues to evolve as agents introduce different kinds of mistakes and as fixes reveal problems earlier reviews missed. “The nature of bugs keeps evolving, so does our benchmark as the models get better,” indicates Harjot.

Better price-performance from OpenAI models has helped CodeRabbit move capabilities from research into its product. Harjot points to improvements in model pricing and caching that let the manufacturer use more AI, add more subagents, and pass the benefits to customers.

It has been revealed that when CodeRabbit started, it used one or two subagents for code navigation. Lower-cost models such as GPT‑6 Luna now support more subagents throughout the platform, while models such as GPT‑6 Astra handle planning and orchestration.

“Now we are using agents everywhere on the use cases we couldn't even afford in the past,” Harjot says. That expands the validation CodeRabbit can perform and the explanations it can give developers, helping them understand and trust changes they did not write themselves.

Sources indicate that by using Codex, Harjot indicates the company has been shipping roughly 20 times more software over the last 6 months without adding engineers. He personally estimates that he pushed 2,500 to 3,000 pull requests in the 30 days before the interview.

In a recent development, getting there required more than adopting Codex. Running multiple agents exposed constraints across the development process, from laptop memory and compute to testing, the tools that compile and package software, and dependencies.

It has been revealed that the team streamlined its release process and reconsidered where human approvals belonged, while using CodeRabbit to automatically ship low-risk changes that didn’t need human intervention. “We had to actually completely rethink the entire software delivery,” Harjot claims.

The firm has also built a Codex-powered Slack bot that triages production incidents, Slack messages, and support tickets. It can return a pull request for the team to review and merge. Harjot sees cloud-based development as a way to reduce local-machine constraints and give teams stronger controls over access and auditing.

It has been revealed that codeRabbit uses Codex for work beyond engineering, including managing marketing and operational tasks through code. “We are running the tech giant as code as much as possible,” Harjot says.

In marketing, the firm manages Google Ads through pull requests. The team opens and merges a request to deploy ads. It also uses a content studio repository where Codex creates slide decks and customer-facing documents. “If you can translate your marketing problems to code problems, you will run 10x faster,” Harjot indicates.

CodeRabbit has run agents in sandbox environments since 2023, cloning repositories and letting agents write code to help perform reviews. More recently, CodeRabbit used OpenAI’s Cyber model through Daybreak to test and secure its own platform.

It has been revealed that the team used the model for internal penetration testing, probing its own platform for ways an attacker could break in. Harjot says the early access helped CodeRabbit secure its own stack. “We found multiple vulnerabilities, advanced hacks that we could not even imagine could happen,” Harjot says.

Sources indicate that it has since taken those capabilities to market, helping secure its customers’ code with its latest product, CodeRabbit Secure. Over the past two weeks, the manufacturer ran a promotional offer where it covered $1M in free deep scans for their users and found over 43,000 security vulnerabilities across 13,000 deep scans, all powered by Codex models. Thousands of these vulnerabilities have already been fixed by its customers, helping improve their code security.

As background agents begin responding to alerts and incidents without a person initiating every task, Harjot expects teams to need more help deciding which changes to take to completion.

Looking ahead, CodeRabbit is expanding toward agentic software development, helping teams validate, prioritize, explain, secure, and verify agent-generated code changes at scale.

The opportunity is to help developers stay in control as agents do more of the building, with validation, explanations, and maintenance that keep pace with the code being produced.

CreditFilter: Calibrated Token Weights over the Within-Response Entropy Rank for RLVR

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (249 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.27227v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Critic-free reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically assigns a uniform advantage to every token. Token-reweighting heuristics like the 80/20 mask favor high-entropy tokens, but fail to measure a token's actual impact on the outcome. We formalize this impact as the forking value: the variance of the success probability over the policy's next-token choices. The expected forking values along a response sum exactly to the reward variance. Token credit is thus, in expectation over a prompt's responses, a fixed budget spent at the forks. This motivates weights that redistribute credit within a response. The forking value factorizes into a fork consequence, which requires costly continuations to estimate, and a fork probability, which the softmax provides. On Qwen3-8B-Base, this fork probability decays exponentially with a token's within-response entropy rank at class-specific rates, revealing that most tokens carry negligible forking value. CreditFilter weights each token by an exponential window over the same rank. The window is calibrated to this fork-probability envelope, under an approximately flat fork consequence. CreditFilter needs no extra forward passes and is stabilized by difficulty damping and an entropy-gated fallback. Averaged over three seeds, it outperforms DAPO by 7.7 points on MATH500 and by 10.5 and 9.1 points on AIME24 and AIME25. Its dynamically adaptive variant matches it. The ablations show that both parts matter: ranking tokens within each response rather than across the batch, and matching the window's decay rate to the envelope. Code is available at https://github.com/yoctta/CreditFilter.

NavTTT: Adaptive Parametric Memory via Hierarchical Test-Time Training for Vision-and-Language Navigation

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (214 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.27219v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) demands that agents accumulate and reason over streaming visual observations throughout long navigation episodes. Existing approaches struggle to maintain long-term history, constrained by the finite context capacity of transformer architectures. To solve the problem, fast-weight test-time training (TTT) provides a mechanism for encoding streaming observations into an evolving parameter state. However, existing TTT does not distinguish informative observations from repetitive visual content, allowing redundant tokens to interfere with the retention of information needed for subsequent decisions. We propose Navigation-Conditioned Test-Time Training (NavTTT), which introduces adaptive memory formation and hierarchical memory integration for vision-and-language navigation. NavTTT leverages global navigation context to prioritize informative visual evidence and integrates language instructions with spatial information to construct spatially grounded memory representations. Episode-local nonlinear fast weights store these representations as Adaptive Parametric Memory (APM), preserving history beyond the visual context for later decisions. To reduce cross-layer coupling in memory formation, NavTTT maintains independent fast-weight memories across multiple decoder depths. This decoupled design prevents errors or biases from spreading across different memory levels. Meanwhile, it enables shared historical information to be independently represented at various levels of abstraction. Experiments demonstrate strong navigation performance on VLN-CE benchmarks and effective instruction following on a real robot.

#24473. Control Room: A central system to track and stop model workloads across our research infrastructure

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1282 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

Control Room: A central system to track and stop model workloads across our research infrastructure

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1282 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As our models get more powerful and the associated safety and security risks become bigger, it becomes more and more critical that we can detect potential concerns, and quickly stop models in their tracks when needed.
  • According to recent reports, control Room is a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them rapidly when safety or security concerns arise.
  • Control Room is already deployed across our research infrastructure, where the need is greatest.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As our models get more powerful and the associated safety and security risks become bigger, it becomes more and more critical that we can detect potential concerns, and quickly stop models in their tracks when needed. To solve this, we built Control Room.

According to recent reports, control Room is a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them rapidly when safety or security concerns arise. It connects every research inference workload, including agentic sampling for model training and evaluation, data processing, and more. This works together with our misalignment monitoring systems, and halts model output within 35 seconds of a decision to intervene to stop or pause a job. It has been built to keep working even when other systems fail, and to stop model output if Control Room itself goes down.

Control Room is already deployed across our research infrastructure, where the need is greatest. Our external model-serving stack is already much more centralized by nature, with a well-developed operational capability to promptly take down model deployments if needed.

Control Room works by integrating a few systems: the workload, the inference engine, and the centralized Control Room service.

Industry observers note that the workload is the job being run, such as a reinforcement learning experiment, an evaluation, a high-volume sampling or data processing job. We require every research workload that does agentic inference to be associated with an approved safety case.

The inference engine, or just engine, is the model itself. You can think of the engine as the brain of the model, running directly on GPUs. A workload normally uses one or more models, which might be running on one or more different inference engines. The same inference engine might be used by more than one different workload.

According to recent reports, the Control Room service tracks jobs and controls whether they are allowed to continue generating model output. Engines check with the Control Room service before fulfilling a request. If a job has been stopped, the service denies the request, preventing further output.

Control Room is integrated in the following way:.

When starting a newly introduced job, the workload code requests a new job_id from Control Room.

Recent findings suggest that whenever the workload needs to sample tokens from a model, it makes a request to an inference engine running that model, passing the job_id. The engine requests permission from Control Room to fulfill that request, passing the job_id along to Control Room.

In a recent development, control Room checks whether that job has been terminated, and if so, it denies the inference request. The engine responds to the workload's inference request with a refusal, stopping further model output from being produced for that job.

The process starts with a researcher launching a job—for example, an experiment or an evaluation.

Industry observers note that job code (or workload code) is owned and run by researchers. Inference engines might be started as part of this job, or standalone engines which are not associated with any particular job might already be running.

The workload code requests a job ID, associating the job with an approved safety case. The job itself makes this request.

Control Room records the job and returns its identifier. The workload will attach this same ID to its inference requests.

The request includes the job_id. This request is made directly from the workload code and does not pass through Control Room.

Before fulfilling the request, the inference engine asks Control Room whether this job is still authorized to run.

Industry observers note that the job is still authorized, so Control Room grants permission. The inference engine can now fulfill the request.

Sources indicate that the model generates a response and the engine sends it back to the research job. The job can use that output and continue its work.

A person or monitoring system tells Control Room to stop this job. Control Room marks its ID as stopped. The workload code remains running.

We do not rely on the workload code to correctly perform a check of whether or not the job is still running.

The engine asks Control Room for permission to fulfill the upcoming inference request, passing along the same job ID.

It has been revealed that when the engine checks permission again, Control Room denies the stopped job. The engine must refuse the inference request.

The engine returns a refusal instead of model output. The research process may remain alive, and the engine remains available to other authorized jobs.

All of our frontier reinforcement learning jobs run with a monitor. A monitor is another model which inspects everything that the model-being-trained is doing, and raises an alert if it detects a problem. For example, our recent DNS-related incident⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) was caught by a monitor.

Control Room and our monitoring system are integrated in the following way:.

If the monitoring system detects a potential issue, depending on the details and severity, the monitoring system may decide to stop the job.

In a recent development, in this case, the monitoring system sends a message to Control Room to stop the job, passing the job_id. Control Room records that the job is terminated.

Next time the job having that job_id makes an inference request to sample more tokens from any model running on any engine, the request will be denied, stopping further model output.

The maximum time between the moment when Control Room receives an instruction to stop a job, and the moment when further progress is no longer possible, is 35 seconds. The 35-second lag comes from a caching layer for inference authorization, to support the required volume of traffic. We are working to drive this number down to zero so that we can end jobs instantly.

Workloads, including experiments, evaluation jobs, etc., are normally owned and operated by researchers or teams of researchers. As a result, workload code changes often, and is not an ideal place to implement critical load-bearing safety protections. Because of this, our implementation is designed to be resilient to buggy or broken workload code.

We achieve this by implementing the termination mechanism in the inference layer. Workload code is highly-varied and decentralized. In contrast, there are only a very small number of inference code paths in use across all of OpenAI research, and their deployments are much more centralized and uniform. This means that the inference layer can serve as a bottleneck, where we can get strong guarantees that all model inference running in research is subject to Control Room authorization checks on every inference request. We additionally run continual agentic and programmatic sweeps to check that owners are not accidentally or maliciously launching rogue engine implementations with Control Room unimplemented or disabled.

According to recent reports, finally, our system “fails closed”, meaning that the Control Room integration in the engines is configured in such a way that if the Control Room service goes down, either due to a system error or because it is disabled for any other reason, including tampering by a bad actor, then all inference requests will be denied until Control Room resumes normal operation. Fail-closed is rolled out now to all frontier model research workloads, and will finish rolling out across all remaining research workloads over the next few days.

In a recent development, control Room is just one part of our holistic approach to safe frontier model training and deployment. We’ll continue to strengthen and expand the system over the coming months, alongside our investments in monitoring for misaligned behavior and security breaches. If you want to help build systems for the safe and secure development and deployment of AGI, we're⁠ hiring⁠!

Correct Precedents Induce Policy Violations in On-Device LLM Agents

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (220 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.27216v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Local-cloud agent systems pair a cloud model with a small on-device agent that acts on private data, often as the last check before an irreversible action. We identify, for the first time, a failure in which such an agent is led into a violation by its own correct decisions within a session. After it correctly releases an item whose restriction was lifted, it becomes more likely to release the next item that is still restricted. Because the trigger is a correct decision, a history with no faulty step can still end in a violation. We call this failure correct-precedent generalization and find it in 13 open-weight models from nine developers. A single correct precedent can cut the safe rate of the most affected agent roughly in half, and the risk compounds when a refused request is simply sent again in a new session. Interventions on the agent's history indicate that it carries its decision on the released item over to the restricted one instead of checking that item's status. Building on this finding, we propose Paired Decision Distillation (PDD), which distills the decisions of a weakly affected teacher into a LoRA adapter. PDD restores the safe rate to nearly 100% in every distilled model, without extra prompt text or model calls.

As for every commercial system added since Podonos retired its API runner, the ARCAS predictions were submitted by Neural Defend and scored by Podonos against its private labels. We describe the benchmark's construction and protocol in full, reproduce the complete leaderboard and its history across five releases, and analyse error balance, statistical separation, speed, and the gap between commercial and open-source detectors. The results agree with the companion evaluation of ARCAS 290M on the complete test sets of ten public benchmarks and establish ARCAS as the most accurate AI-generated audio detector evaluated on this independent benchmark.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.27211v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Personalized long-form generation asks a language model to write new text the way a specific user would. The standard recipe, retrieval-augmented generation, places a few of the user's past texts in the prompt but leaves the model to decide what to take from them. We introduce StylePrism, a taxonomy of 28 stylistic aspects in seven categories, and SP-Refine, an inference-time method that makes style extraction an explicit step: the model first fills StylePrism with the user's patterns, quoted evidence, and habits to avoid, then drafts from the user's samples and revises the draft twice against this profile, guided by its own style scores. On the three long-form tasks of LongLaMP with three LLMs, SP-Refine outperforms LongLaMP's retrieval-augmented baseline in 25 of 27 ROUGE and METEOR comparisons, by 10.2% on average and by up to 35.8%. Annotating people' own texts with the extracted profiles shows that StylePrism captures concrete, checkable habits, from the order of rhetorical moves to a reviewer's sign-off. Ablations show that the profile helps as revision guidance, not as a replacement for the samples: writing from the profile alone is worse in all 27 comparisons, while a single implicit-inference call is a cheaper alternative that comes close. Oracle variants that let the reviser see the reference, together with reference-free controls, show that larger refinement gains require information unavailable at inference time.

Cogent combines OpenAI models with enterprise context to help automatically remediate vulnerabilities with agents.

Lower mean time to remediate vulnerabilities.

In a recent development, as Cogent Security⁠(opens in a latest window) sees enterprises facing more security risks than ever, it has found that the hardest part is not finding vulnerabilities, but fixing them. Remediation work is complex and spans multiple teams. It requires contextual understanding of a firm’s environment: how could an attacker exploit a vulnerability, which business systems are at stake, and what changes can be made safely.

According to recent reports, cogent builds Cyber Defense Factories for enterprises to autonomously find and eliminate those risks. The factories are designed to help defenders move at machine speed, in response to the acceleration in vulnerability discovery and exploitation.

It has been revealed that the company’s AI agents combine GPT‑6.1 Sol and GPT‑5.6 with its enterprise context and controls to handle investigation through verified remediation. The agents assess exposures, execute permitted changes, and confirm the risk has been eliminated. Cogent also conducts internal research with Cyber and Daybreak, exploring attack paths and defensive capabilities.

For each customer, Cogent’s Context Engine maintains an enterprise knowledge graph of assets, vulnerabilities, identities, ownership, and dependencies. Specialized background agents continuously reconcile information across security tools and systems, giving investigation and remediation agents a shared understanding of the environment.

Recent findings suggest that GPT‑6 Astra handles upfront planning and complex reasoning for that work. This enables what Geng Sng, Co-founder and CTO of Cogent, describes as a “memory harness for the enterprise.” He notes, “We don’t have to relearn what the world looks like every time a new task happens.” Reusing context reduces latency, inference costs, and inconsistent results.

In a recent development, cogent’s Agent Policies define each enterprise’s permitted changes and approval requirements, and its policy-enforcement engine, TRACE, checks tool calls against the policies before execution. The checks are deterministic and require no separate model inference.

Recent findings suggest that an Agent Gateway independently checks authorization, and higher-risk work can run in isolated sandboxes. Customers can delegate investigation, require approval for changes, or permit bounded autonomous remediation.

When critical security flaws known as PHP2Shell were disclosed in PHP, a programming language used to run websites, customers turned to the Cyber Defense Factories that Cogent had already deployed in their environments.

GPT‑6.1 Sol and GPT‑6 Astra provided the deep reasoning for investigation and remediation planning. Using Cogent’s context layer, agents identified affected systems, assessed exposure, and developed looks that accounted for application dependencies and operational constraints. Then they orchestrated fixes using customer-defined approval and execution workflows and verified the resolution.

Industry observers note that cogent reports that customers are using its Cyber Defense Factories to resolve vulnerabilities faster and expand investigation capacity. With Cogent, a Fortune 1000 automotive customer reduced its mean time to remediate critical vulnerabilities by 75%, and a Fortune 500 IT services customer achieved 5× vulnerability-triage throughput.

Global electronic trading platform MarketAxess leverages Cogent to help strengthen its risk-based approach to exposure management. “Cogent brings together vulnerability data, business context, security controls, and attack path analysis to help us validate real exposures and prioritize remediation where it matters most. What stands out is how rapidly the Cogent team responds to emerging threats and turns our feedback into practical capabilities,” says Vijay Bala, CISO, MarketAxess.

In a recent development, cogent continuously evaluates closed-source and open-source alternatives and reports stronger reasoning on long-running security tasks, higher fidelity, fewer hallucinations on technical codebases, and more reliable execution with OpenAI models. The models can chain tool calls sequentially and in parallel while retaining context across remediation workflows.

Recent findings suggest that cogent prioritizes reasoning quality for complex investigations and cost for more straightforward work. It uses GPT‑6.1 Sol for general execution and GPT‑5.6 for routine vulnerability-management tasks where advanced reasoning is less critical.

According to recent reports, using OpenAI models has also reduced the supporting software Cogent needs to build for remediation and patching. “A lot of the work that we had to do at the harness level is no longer required,” Geng claims. He also shared that OpenAI APIs have “streamlined request routing and agent orchestration, significantly reducing internal engineering overhead and accelerating our time-to-market for complex security workflows.”.

In a recent development, most of Cogent’s engineers also choose Codex for development. Geng says they’re more productive pairing Codex with OpenAI models vs. using the same models in an open-source coding environment. “Codex just comes with tools that we don’t have to build ourselves,” says Geng.

In a recent development, through Trusted Access for Cyber and Daybreak, Cogent receives technical support for its internal red-teaming and attack-path research. Daybreak Red, an access tier within Daybreak, provides the team with specialized OpenAI models for authorized offensive and vulnerability research. “Good defense requires good offense,” Geng notes.

Cogent aims to expand its capabilities as the key partner for enterprises to build their own Cyber Defense Factories. Its roadmap includes increasingly autonomous remediation, broadening the range and complexity of fixes agents can execute, from straightforward configuration changes to multi-step workflows spanning different enterprise systems.

The firm is also developing autonomous discovery and validation. Its goal is a closed-loop system that finds and eliminates risk while continuously learning from every vulnerability to improve future investigations and fixes.

An ablation that adds 2,000 manually written, formula-guided samples decreases exact match to 42.32%, exposing a domain-alignment matter rather than an automatic benefit from more data. arXiv:2611.27206v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Clinical monitoring and wearable devices capture complementary physiological signals, but their partially overlapping modality coverage makes within-signal information and cross-modal relationships difficult to exploit jointly. We introduce LingSante-Pulse, a unified, general-purpose and flexible physiological representation framework that learns from these heterogeneous recordings. A shared, signal-conditioned encoder processes each physical channel independently and supports different numbers and combinations of signals for multimodal assessment and single-sensor inference. Pairwise cross-modal alignment, structured random-feature prediction (RFP) and masked waveform reconstruction jointly learn physiological relationships and preserve informative within-signal structure. Across 38 general physiological task configurations spanning PPG, ECG, EEG and EMG, the frozen encoder achieves the best dataset-balanced mean rank in each domain. In sleep assessment, multimodal staging on the HMC dataset and EEG-only staging on the Sleep-EDF dataset reach Macro-F1 scores of 0.7784 and 0.7941, respectively, while single-lead ECG apnea screening achieves an AUROC of 0.9183. Controlled experiments show that function prediction and waveform reconstruction provide complementary supervision for retaining temporal and rhythmic information. Representations learned under continually refreshed random supervision generalize to unseen teacher realizations, and correct auxiliary modality correspondence improves respiration-only representations. These results demonstrate that a single encoder can learn reusable physiological features across signal types, prediction targets and sensor configurations from partially overlapping recordings.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (247 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

arXiv:2611.27198v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: State-of-the-art multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) models rely on large pretrained encoders, yet typically process every modality to its full depth, regardless of its computational cost or predictive contribution. This raises a fundamental question: how should limited computation be allocated across modalities to preserve predictive performance? We reveal a substantial mismatch between the computational cost of modality encoders and the predictive benefit of processing them more deeply, suggesting that different modalities require different encoding depths. However, enabling heterogeneous depths introduces a key challenge: representations extracted at different depths must still be effectively fused. To address this, we propose $\textbf{DepthMSA}$, a budget-aware framework that supports flexible modality depths within a single MSA model. Specifically, we introduce combinatorial anytime training, which supervises the fusion head across all cross-modal depth combinations using a single full-depth encoder pass. At inference, a training-free, cost-aware allocator selects the configuration with the lowest validation-calibrated error under a sample-specific FLOPs budget. On CMU-MOSEI, DepthMSA maintains accuracy within one percentage point of the full-depth model while reducing measured FLOPs by 45\%, or by 82\% with a separately trained skip-enabled variant. When a CLIP visual encoder dominates computation, the allocation shifts toward reducing visual depth, achieving 56\% fewer FLOPs at unchanged accuracy. Compared with ADMN, an adaptive layer-allocation method that trains a controller for each budget, the skip-enabled variant reaches its accuracy with 3.2$\times$ fewer FLOPs and lower latency, without any per-budget training. Our project is available at https://pwang322.github.io/DepthMSA/.

Work at the Frontier: AI’s effect on freelance work

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (820 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • New research from OpenAI and Upwork finds shifting demand for freelance services, new combinations of skills, and larger budgets for AI-related projects.
  • It has been revealed that for freelancers, changes in the market arrive one assignment at a time: a client needs a different service, requests a new skill or expands a project’s scope.
  • According to recent reports, the stakes are substantial.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New research from OpenAI and Upwork finds shifting demand for freelance services, new combinations of skills, and larger budgets for AI-related projects.

It has been revealed that for freelancers, changes in the market arrive one assignment at a time: a client needs a different service, requests a new skill or expands a project’s scope. Our new research with Upwork offers an early view of these changes in the AI era. Some familiar services are losing market share, while AI-related projects bring together different capabilities—and involve larger budgets and more hours of work.

According to recent reports, the stakes are substantial. Upwork’s 2026 Future Workforce Index⁠(opens in a latest window) found that 38% of skilled U.S. knowledge workers freelance. Its previous annual study⁠(opens in a new window) estimated that freelance knowledge work generated $1.5 trillion in U.S. earnings in 2024. Those estimates extend well beyond Upwork’s own marketplace.

Freelance work can also reveal changes sooner than economy-wide employment statistics. Contracts are often short, and clients can adjust their requirements with each posting. To get to the root of these changes, we partnered with Upwork, an online marketplace connecting clients and freelancers, to study those requests alongside the activities people undertake directly with ChatGPT.

Sources indicate that the mix of work differed across the two platforms. Writing accounted for a much larger share of ChatGPT use, while video and animation accounted for larger shares of requests for freelancers in Upwork postings.

Below are the ranges of tasks between the two platforms.

These activities represent only the largest changes in Upwork shares over the studied period. ChatGPT shares cover Jan 2025–Jun 2026; Upwork shares are H1 2026. Changes in Upwork share are H1 2025 to H1 2026, in percentage points.

Sources indicate that many activities that were relatively common in ChatGPT lost share on Upwork, while less common activities gained share. Of the 63 work categories analyzed, 43 followed this pattern.

The remaining 20 work categories showed the reverse. ChatGPT use alone does not explain changes in freelance demand.

The comparison also captures how people currently use ChatGPT, not the full range of tasks AI can support—a gap OpenAI calls the capability overhang.

Sources indicate that each point represents one of 63 matched work subcategories in the Upwork taxonomy. The horizontal axis is the natural log of the category’s share of ChatGPT use in H2 2025 divided by its share of Upwork job posts in H1 2023. The vertical axis shows the percentage change in the category’s share of Upwork postings from H1 2023 to H2 2025, on a logarithmic scale; 0% indicates unchanged marketplace share. The vertical divider at AI intensity 0 marks equal category shares in ChatGPT and baseline Upwork postings.

Sources indicate that by late 2025, clients were requesting the use of AI in many more, different kinds of work. Clients were seeking freelancers to apply AI in tasks including chatbot development, video production, marketing automation, and application integration.

Industry observers note that within individual projects, AI capabilities were often requested alongside other work. AI-related postings listed about as many tasks as other postings but more often combined tasks that had rarely appeared together in earlier jobs.

Recent findings suggest that some clients asked for AI-generated video, editing, and motion graphics in a single posting. The freelancer would bring those skills together to deliver a finished video.

Between early 2023 and late 2025, the mix of tasks in AI-related postings became 45% more diverse—the equivalent of an increase from about 15 equally common tasks to about 21.

Sources indicate that although posted hourly rates were similar for AI-related and other work, AI-related projects had larger fixed-price budgets and involved more hours of work. This pattern suggests that higher budgets may partly reflect a broader scope of work.

In a recent development, AI’s effects on work can be difficult to detect in employment statistics. As we have noted in previous Work at the Frontier papers, the effects may appear first in the work people do.

Recent findings suggest that because freelance projects turn over quickly, postings are continually refreshed as clients’ needs change. Work within firms can evolve without appearing in a fresh job posting. Combined with ChatGPT data, these postings offer an early view of which activities people undertake directly with AI, which they hire freelancers to perform, and how AI-related projects differ from other work.

The findings do not point to a simple substitution story. Some activities common in ChatGPT use lost share on Upwork, but this pattern was not uniform. AI-related work also spanned a wider mix of activities, combined tasks in less familiar ways, and carried larger fixed-price budgets and more hours. Together, these patterns suggest that AI may be shifting both what clients seek from freelancers and how they assemble projects.

The OpenAI Economic Research Team explores how AI is changing work in real time with the Work at the Frontier series.

A Frugal AI Framework for India: Responsible and Right-sized AI

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (268 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2611.27189v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: India's AI debate often swings between two insufficient options: replicating the compute-intensive, capital-heavy foundation-model programmes of the United States or China, or remaining a downstream adopter of foreign AI with localised interfaces and safeguards. Neither serves a country that must deliver AI to a very large, diverse population across uneven infrastructure and within constrained budgets. This white paper from the Centre for Responsible AI (CeRAI), IIT Madras, proposes a third path: Responsible Frugal AI, which applies principle-based frugal engineering alongside Responsible AI. Responsible Frugal AI is right-sized AI: it fixes the functional requirement first, asks whether AI is needed at all, and then chooses the smallest sufficient model, meeting the requirement with minimal resources while keeping a verified margin, robustness and responsible governance. The framework applies frugality across four dimensions (data, compute, model and operations) through seven levers spanning the AI lifecycle, each with practices and measures. It calls for public AI rails, vernacular-first design, measured resource use, human oversight for high-stakes decisions, and a cap on total resource consumption so that efficiency gains are not cancelled out by rising usage. We argue that India is resource-imbalanced rather than resource-poor, and that frugal principles offer the most viable route to population-scale deployment, fit naturally with India's digital public infrastructure, and make sovereignty operational by preserving India's capacity to specify, deploy, govern, inspect and adapt its AI systems. A seven-point adoption checklist and eleven policy statements translate the framework into practice, positioning AI in India as a responsible, frugal public-value system that maximises social value per rupee and per joule.

AI is becoming part of how Singapore Airlines serves customers, empowers employees, and builds technology. The airline uses the OpenAI API for customer-facing experiences and OpenAI models inside Jarvis, its governed internal AI platform for employees. It also uses OpenAI models in its software development workflows to deliver more personalized service, improve productivity, and help teams build more efficiently.

Across these deployments, Singapore Airlines pairs OpenAI models with orchestration, internal data controls, validation, and human review, giving teams a consistent way to bring AI into production workflows responsibly.

One of Singapore Airlines’ most visible AI applications is Kris, its customer-facing chatbot. After moving Kris from a traditional dialog-flow system to an LLM-powered conversational experience using the OpenAI API, Singapore Airlines saw a 2x increase in customer satisfaction.

In a recent development, alongside that, the airline deployed AI-assisted tools for customer service representatives, including OpenAI API-powered call summarization, so that representatives spend less time on after-call work and more time on the customer. Singapore Airlines saw an approximately 10% reduction in average handling time for its customer service representatives.

In the earlier dialog-flow based chatbot design, every topic had to be mapped manually, and every flow had to be written in advance. That made coverage difficult to scale. If an intent was missing, the conversation was more likely to end up requiring support from a customer service representative, even when the customer’s request could have been handled through self-service.

According to recent reports, singapore Airlines moved Kris to a fully LLM-powered conversational experience using the OpenAI API. Instead of depending on predefined flows, the chatbot can interpret customer intent in natural language, ground answers in a knowledge base, manage multi-topic conversations, and hand over to a customer service representative with the relevant context when needed.

Sources indicate that today, customers use Kris for general queries, special requests, real-time flight disruption information, and selected transactional workflows. Singapore Airlines is continuing to expand its capabilities to include booking changes, baggage transactions, and more complex agentic interactions.

Flight Recommender lets customers describe the trip they want in natural language instead of repeatedly adjusting filters, dates, and destinations. Usage has grown nearly 3x over the past year.

Built on the OpenAI API, Flight Recommender uses an orchestration layer connected to fare and availability data. It interprets customer intent, calls the relevant tools, and returns personalized travel recommendations in natural language.

Sources indicate that the team has also implemented guardrails for input and output validation, malicious or inappropriate query handling, hallucination reduction, PII handling, and authenticated access to only the context required for each query. Singapore Airlines is preparing to expand the experience into a more conversational chatbot interaction, where customers can keep refining travel ideas rather than restarting a search.

Beyond customer-facing experiences, Singapore Airlines is also using OpenAI models in parts of the software development lifecycle to help teams blueprint, refine, test, and review work more efficiently. Across selected software development lifecycle activities, teams have achieved productivity gains of up to 20%.

AI now runs through the entire delivery lifecycle and not just coding. Teams use generative AI models to support requirements refinement, stakeholder-session analysis, product specifications, edge-case identification, test-case creation, architecture review, and the breakdown of complex work into smaller, more testable tasks.

For one commercial feature, the team used the OpenAI API to challenge assumptions, identify ambiguous requirements and surface edge cases before development begins. Once those were well-defined, AI helped translate them into design options, implementation plans, test cases and then code generation.

During deployment and beyond, AI also helps to interpret how the system is behaving in production, and flagging concerns that might otherwise go unnoticed. With AI active at every step of the workflow, team members have shifted from producing every artifact themselves, to directing, reviewing and validating what AI produces throughout the delivery lifecycle. This means they can focus on work that truly requires human judgement, such as prioritization, architecture, governance and stakeholder outcomes.

It has been revealed that more broadly, OpenAI models are helping Singapore Airlines improve requirements quality, test coverage, and conformance with internal standards. Teams use these workflows to generate edge cases for testing, review architecture plans, and support human validation before work moves further through the development lifecycle.

Sources indicate that beyond engineering teams, Singapore Airlines is making AI accessible across the business through Jarvis, its internal AI platform. Powered by OpenAI models, Jarvis gives employees a governed way to use AI in their day-to-day work, from summarizing documents to creating custom workflows.

According to recent reports, employees use Jarvis to work across PDFs, Word documents, Excel files, PowerPoint decks, and other file types in a secure environment, while creating custom workflows and lightweight knowledge bases for their day-to-day work. Today, more than 60% of Singapore Airlines employees are using Jarvis monthly with adoption continuing to increase.

Flight Recommender is moving toward a more conversational travel discovery experience, where customers can refine ideas over multiple turns rather than restarting a search.

Together with its customer-facing innovations, this is helping the airline build a future where AI makes travel more seamless, employees more productive, and the business more responsive to changing needs.

GEG-SAM: Gaze Exploration-Guided Segment Anything Model for Weakly Supervised Polyp Segmentation

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (239 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.27183v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Endoscopist gaze offers an unobtrusively acquired record of lesion-oriented visual exploration during routine clinical inspection, providing relevant supervision for tasks. However, existing methods treat fixations as isolated spatial prompts directly associated with the target, overlooking the fact that natural gaze records a continuous visual search process in which fixations are temporally connected, spatially organized, and coupled with the visual content. Interpreting each fixation independently based only on its local visual content overlooks the temporal evolution and spatial organization of the gaze trajectory, whereas modeling relations among fixations alone cannot reveal the visual semantics of the regions they attend to. To this end, we propose the Gaze Exploration-Guided Segment Anything Model (GEG-SAM), a principled weakly supervised framework designed to explicitly exploit structured gaze relations and their corresponding visual cues to modulate SAM for polyp segmentation. Specifically, GEG-SAM captures structured gaze relations by modeling the temporal dynamics and spatial topology of gaze exploration. It then associates these relational representations with fixation-aligned visual context to derive gaze-conditioned tokens, which are further injected into the frozen SAM encoder to modulate its pretrained image features. In this way, GEG-SAM effectively exploits the rich information embedded in gaze exploration to guide SAM toward lesion-oriented segmentation. Extensive experiments on five public polyp segmentation datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, improving the mean Dice by 9.30 percentage points over the strongest weakly supervised baseline.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.27175v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) enables non-interactive, privacy-preserving transformer fine-tuning, protecting highly sensitive data as inputs to large language models. Prior work has predominantly pursued efficiency gains through architectural refinements, yet overall performance remains bounded by the substantial cost inherent in encrypted computation. To address these problems, we target the bottleneck at the ciphertext operation level. Concretely, we propose a novel packing strategy that supports batching over a flexible number of inputs, making it well-suited for fine-tuning workloads. In addition, we design operation-specific matrix evaluation algorithms that significantly reduce (i) the number of ciphertext rotations and relinearizations, and (ii) the number of bootstrapping invocations. Additionally, we exploit functional bootstrapping to fold the evaluation of element-wise activation functions directly into the bootstrapping step, thereby reducing overall computational complexity. As a result, our framework achieves a $30\times$ reduction in ciphertext rotations and relinearizations across all matrix operations, as well as a $2.5\times$ reduction in FHE bootstrapping invocations over the entire computation flow, compared to the latest state-of-the-art work. It is worth noting that our system completes fine-tuning of a 2-layer BERT-style model with a batch size of 16 in 650 seconds, achieving a $8\times$ speedup over the state-of-the-art work.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Drawing on fresh ThinkYoung research and lessons from our EMEA partnerships to support independent learning with AI.
  • AI is prompting a fundamental reassessment of what education should prepare societies for.
  • Recent findings suggest that across EMEA, we are working with governments and education systems, including in Estonia, Slovakia, Greece and Italy, amongst others to explore how AI can support educators.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Drawing on fresh ThinkYoung research and lessons from our EMEA partnerships to support independent learning with AI.

AI is prompting a fundamental reassessment of what education should prepare societies for. As intelligence becomes easier to access and apply, the question is no longer simply what people need to know, but which skills and capabilities will help them thrive in an AI-enabled world. Recent debates around PISA and AI, including those led by the OECD’s Andreas Schleicher⁠(opens in a new window), underscore this shift. They also point to a central lesson: as AI becomes more capable, the role of teachers becomes more important, not less. Their expertise, judgement and ability to guide learning remain essential. Equipping teachers, schools and governments with AI skills and confidence to make informed decisions about these tools must therefore be a priority for education systems.

Recent findings suggest that across EMEA, we are working with governments and education systems, including in Estonia, Slovakia, Greece and Italy, amongst others to explore how AI can support educators. These collaborations share three priorities: equitable access to frontier AI tools, jointly designed AI literacy programmes, and ongoing measurement and evaluation, whilst adapting to local languages, curricula and institutions.

This report shares emerging lessons from our education partnerships in EMEA, focusing on educator support, AI literacy, local capability and evaluation. It examines what partners have tried, what they have reported and what remains uncertain. Country examples reflect their particular contexts and arrangements, and their findings should be interpreted within those limits. Five themes organise these lessons: clear educational goals, educator preparation, local partnerships, critical AI literacy and credible evidence.

Three early patterns are emerging from this work:.

Country partnerships offer context-specific lessons. Experiences in Estonia, Greece and Slovakia point to three lessons that other education systems can apply: strong public leadership to set a clear direction, investment in teachers' skills and confidence, and practical support tailored to local curricula and classroom needs. While implementation will vary across countries, these principles offer a useful foundation for governments seeking to integrate AI responsibly and at scale.

Closing the AI guidance gap in education is becoming increasingly urgent. New research from ThinkYoung,⁠(opens in a new window) which examines the ways teachers and students are already engaging with AI highlights a clear guidance gap: 79% of surveyed students reported using AI for homework or assignments, but only 47% reported being shown how. Governments need to support educators and give students clearer expectations. Below we set out how educators can be better supported to set the terms and conditions of use.

Sources indicate that early benefits for teachers are clear. Adoption and reported time savings for teachers are encouraging. Understanding where AI strengthens knowledge, independent thinking and retention requires sustained evaluation and through the government actions that we observed, we identify how to prioritise more research into this critical area.

According to recent reports, our aim is to share practical lessons from these partnerships that education leaders can consider in their own contexts. These are early experiences, rather than a single model for education systems to follow.

We are also learning how to judge progress with evidence: teacher adoption and reported time savings offer encouraging early signals. Surveys, programme monitoring and consultation help us understand participants’ experiences and the barriers they encounter.

Sources indicate that at OpenAI, our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits everyone. Helping learners flourish is central to that ambition. We believe that every young person should have the opportunity to develop the skills to participate in a world increasingly shaped by AI, whatever their background or wherever they attend school. We have a responsibility to contribute to that evidence and learn openly from the findings, including when they challenge our assumptions. Through the OpenAI Learning Lab, we are bringing education researchers together to understand when and how AI can support education systems.

The choices made today will shape how the next generation learns, works and participates in society. With ambition, care, public leadership and a commitment to evidence, AI can help extend educational opportunity and strengthen young people’s capacity to understand, create and act for themselves.

Tech Report: Co-Evolving Behavioral Agents and Detectors for Adaptive Information Operations

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (292 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.27156v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Detectors of state-sponsored information operations (IOs) are trained on campaigns that platforms have already taken down. They lose much of their accuracy on an actor they have not seen, even though no operator in the archived data is trying to avoid them. A real operator wants two things, to reach an audience and to avoid being caught. We present IO-AI, a framework that gives simulated agents these two capabilities, engagement and evasion, and tests what each one does to detection. The agents are built from the posting behavior of real campaigns and choose the emotion, type, and timing of each post. An agent and a detector then train against each other in turn. We rank the trained agents by how hard they are to detect and train one detector on them from easiest to hardest. On 20 Twitter IO campaigns, this detector reduces missed detections of adaptive agents by 65% relative to a detector trained only on the archived campaigns, at a similar false-alarm rate. On actors it has never seen it reaches an F1 of 0.81, against 0.62. We find that an agent trained to seek engagement becomes easier to catch, because it learns the fast, emotional retweeting that archived campaigns were caught producing. An agent that was trained for engagement before the game keeps its engagement lead after it learns to evade. We also introduce a behavioral distance metric that compares two groups of accounts using only their unlabeled posting histories. The larger the distance between two groups, the worse a detector trained on one does on the other (Spearman rho = -0.58), so the metric can be used to choose which latest groups to test first.

Breaking: Structure Over Scale: Rethinking Adaptation for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (235 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.27148v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) is often framed as a choice between the expressivity of Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) and the efficiency of Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). We find that this framing misses an notable variable: the geometry of the update. Under a common cold-start GRPO protocol, LoRA exhibits rank collapse: performance remains broadly stable at low rank, then fails abruptly as rank increases. On DeepMath-Hard, for example, accuracy drops from 73.1% at r=64 to 4.7% at r=128. In contrast, Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation (DoRA) and Quantum-Informed Tensor Adaptation (QuanTA) remain stable over a wider tested optimization region and are competitive with FFT while updating less than 0.6% of the model parameters. Spectral analysis reveals a corresponding difference in learned update structure: collapsed LoRA concentrates its update energy into relatively few effective directions, whereas structured adapters produce substantially more distributed updates. These results suggest that nominal rank and parameter count alone are insufficient to characterize adaptation in RLVR - the structure imposed on the reachable update manifold also matters. Finally, across three 8B base models, adapter behavior aligns with both frozen-weight spectral structure and reported pre-training scale, motivating the Model Maturity Hypothesis: the adaptation geometry that works best may depend on properties already encoded during pre-training. We present this as a falsifiable hypothesis rather than a causal conclusion. The code can be found here https://github.com/Shrimpstanot/structure-over-scale.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Claim your business, keep your information current, and understand how people engage with you in ChatGPT.

Sources indicate that we’re introducing Businesses in ChatGPT in beta, giving businesses a newly introduced way to connect with the 1.2 billion people who use ChatGPT each week. Through Business Hub⁠(opens in a new window), businesses can claim their business, manage their information, and see insights on how people engage with them on ChatGPT. In addition, we are adding a powerful new way for businesses to interact with people via Business Agents, starting with eligible ecommerce and online service businesses in the U.S.

Together, these products create more ways for businesses to connect with people as they explore options and make decisions. They strengthen how people discover and interact with businesses in ChatGPT through broader business coverage, up-to-date information, and the ability to connect with a business through its Business Agent. Throughout these experiences, protecting the trust people place in ChatGPT remains our North Star.

Sources indicate that in Business Hub, companies can claim their organization in ChatGPT and, once verified, upgrade key details and add self-service product feeds with pricing and availability. This gives businesses a upcoming way to provide information to ChatGPT, helping people explore products and services using the most accurate and up-to-date details.

Recent findings suggest that any eligible business located where ChatGPT is available can claim their business in ChatGPT through Business Hub. Existing OpenAI Enterprise customers and advertisers can work directly with their OpenAI representative to claim their business. Shopify merchants can connect their store from Business Hub or the Shopify admin to streamline verification. Eligible products from Shopify merchants are already integrated into ChatGPT through Shopify Catalog.

According to recent reports, business Hub provides aggregated insights into how people engage with a business in ChatGPT. This includes the number of mentions and website clicks a business receives. Businesses can also explore discovery topics—common themes across conversations where their website is cited. These insights can help businesses understand how they’re represented and find opportunities to improve the information they share.

According to recent reports, we’ve designed these insights to protect user privacy. We don’t share users’ conversations or Business Agent chats with businesses. Insights are aggregated and are only available when there are enough conversations or interactions to meet certain thresholds.

After claiming their business in ChatGPT, eligible organizations can build, test, and launch a Business Agent—a new way to answer questions and help people explore their offerings.

When a business appears in a model response, people can click to see the business’s ChatGPT profile. If a Business Agent is available, customers can choose to start a conversation with the business to explore its offerings and ask follow-up questions. For example, someone comparing products could ask about the differences between two options and which features fit their needs. A Business Agent could help them explore those questions using the business’s information.

Industry observers note that for customers, this can make it easier to understand whether an offering is the right fit. For businesses, it creates a way to help interested customers learn more through a personalized conversation. The Business Agent conversation is clearly labeled, separate from the customer’s original ChatGPT conversation, and distinct from ChatGPT’s independent answers.

Businesses can also sponsor their Business Agent⁠ and use it as the destination for ChatGPT Ads to reach more potential customers. Sponsored placements are clearly labeled and separate from ChatGPT responses.

Sources indicate that business Agents are now available to eligible ecommerce and online service businesses in the United States. Learn more about eligible categories here⁠.

As people turn to AI to discover products, compare options and make decisions, ChatGPT has become the platform for people and businesses to connect through AI. Today’s announcement is an early step in bringing businesses more deeply into ChatGPT. We’re starting with the foundations: accurate business information, useful insights, and conversations that help people make informed decisions. Over time, we initiative to expand Businesses in ChatGPT and Business Agents to more markets and business categories, and build tools for organizations with more complex needs.

It has been revealed that as the platform evolves, we’ll explore more ways for businesses to connect with customers—directly or through agents—in ChatGPT and beyond. Our goal is to make ChatGPT more useful for people making decisions, and give businesses new ways to participate and grow.

Learn more and⁠ claim your business in ChatGPT.⁠.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.27142v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Promptable segmentation foundation models are increasingly used in specialized domains, but it remains unclear how SAM-3 should be fine-tuned when adapting it beyond its original training distribution. We study this question by comparing five adaptation families --LoRA, HiRA, KRAdapter, QuanTA, and Full Fine-Tuning-- across five segmentation datasets spanning medical imaging, remote sensing, and dense material segmentation. Across these datasets, compact parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods often match or approach Full Fine-Tuning in DSC and IoU, suggesting that strong in-domain adaptation does not always require updating the full model. However, this performance cannot be explained by nominal adapter rank or trainable parameter count alone. To investigate why different methods perform similarly, we analyze their update spectra and their behavior under LoveDA Urban/Rural transfer. Our SVD analysis shows that Full Fine-Tuning updates are spectrally compressible. However, successful PEFT methods do not simply recover the same update directions; instead, they often concentrate changes in different components and subspaces. The domain-transfer study further shows that methods with similar in-domain performance can respond differently under distribution shift. Together, these results suggest that SAM-3 adaptation is often capacity-saturated in practice, while competitive fine-tuning arises through method-specific update paths rather than a single low-rank approximation to Full Fine-Tuning.

Do Senior Agents Do Their Job? Measuring Role Integrity in How LLM Agents Use Subordinate Material

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (286 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.27139v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly divide long tasks among subagents whose reports a senior agent turns into the final answer. Such a division of labor pays off only if each agent, and above all the senior agent, carries out the duties of its role. Current evaluations, however, mostly score the final answer, and a fluent, well-cited answer cannot show whether the senior agent weighed its subagents' reports or merely aggregated them. To assess whether a senior agent meets its assigned responsibilities, we define role integrity as the preservation of an agent's functional responsibilities when it acts on its subordinates' material. To measure it, we introduce RI-Bench, a behavioral benchmark grounded in the structures and public records of three institutional hierarchies: peer review, appellate adjudication, and parliamentary inquiry. We choose these hierarchies because their rules explicitly assign the senior role a duty toward subordinate material, and together they cover three basic duties: to weigh, to verify, and to relay. Rather than scoring output correctness, we measure how senior agents' outputs respond to controlled changes in subordinate material, using rule-based checks and a rubric-guided LLM judge calibrated against human annotation. Across eight LLMs and over 12,000 agentic episodes, senior agents rarely adopt a planted procedural error (2.9% of rulings) but often follow a majority of generic reviews (up to 71% of decisions) or drop witnesses' stated limitations (up to 65% of cited claims). Obligation prompts reduce these failures without removing them, and they also shift behavior in the control conditions. These findings motivate direct, obligation-specific evaluation of role integrity rather than inferring it from general capability or explicit role instructions. Code and data are available at https://github.com/jxtse/ri-bench.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In collaboration with Caregiver Action Network, Alzheimer’s Association, and American Diabetes Association®, bringing free, hands-on ChatGPT workshops to five U.S. cities during National Family Caregivers Month.

According to recent reports, caregiving often means juggling schedules, keeping track of information, and finding support while balancing work and family life. During National Family Caregivers Month, we’re helping caregivers gain AI skills that can make some of those everyday tasks easier, giving them more time to focus on the people they care for.

On November 10, OpenAI Academy, in collaboration with Caregiver Action Network, Alzheimer’s Association, and American Diabetes Association®, is hosting the AI Skills Jam for Caregivers & Community Health: a free, in-person learning experience designed to help caregivers use ChatGPT confidently, safely, and practically. These nationwide events will bring together participants across five U.S. cities, including individual and family caregivers, caregiver support organizations, and people living with chronic or serious health conditions:.

An OpenAI analysis estimates that more than 40 million weekly ChatGPT messages about healthcare in the U.S. ask about healthcare for someone else1. At the workshops, participants will explore how ChatGPT can help with resource navigation, peer support, and caregiver support, including how to:.

organize caregiver schedules and checklists.

turn trusted educational resources into plain-language materials.

prepare support group discussion guides.

Participants will also learn how to use AI responsibly, including protecting personal information and understanding the limits of these tools. Participants will also learn when to consult healthcare professionals and how AI tools should complement, not replace, medical, legal, or financial advice. OpenAI facilitators and mentors will offer hands-on support throughout the workshops. No coding or technical background is required.

Sources indicate that the Jam brings this learning into local communities, where caregivers can practice alongside peers and share the everyday challenges they hope these tools can help address. Our partners bring deep expertise and experience supporting people living with serious illness and their families. Their perspectives, together with those of caregivers themselves, will help connect the day’s learning to the needs of each community.

The AI Skills Jam is part of OpenAI Academy’s broader work to make AI practical and accessible to everyone. It builds on previous events we’ve hosted with nonprofits, small businesses, K–12 educators, and older adults.

In a recent development, we are grateful to Caregiver Action Network, Alzheimer’s Association, American Diabetes Association®, and the caregivers and community health organizations joining us across the country. Their questions, ideas, and experiences will help shape future learning resources and ensure these tools are useful in the daily work of supporting others.

This is from a privacy-preserving ChatGPT usage estimate for October 9–29, 2026.

arXiv:2611.27106v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to extract records, generate SQL, summarize reports, answer policy questions, and route operational work. At these software boundaries, parseable output is necessary but does not establish task correctness. We present a reproducible benchmark protocol, a public executable artifact, and a confirmatory live API evaluation that separate structural validity from task-specific correctness across five business workflow tasks and six Python implementation conditions: PydanticAI, LangGraph, DSPy, CrewAI, Agno, and a framework-free SDK reference. We hypothesize that (H1) schema validity and task quality are separable, (H2) structured-output binding paths are heterogeneous under a shared model and lowest-common-denominator contract, and (H3) condition-by-task interactions concentrate failures rather than shifting all tasks equally. Confirmatory analysis uses distinct task instances (100 extraction and 50 per other task, with three nested replicates) under a frozen analysis initiative, yielding a 5400-row primary matrix with equivalence margins and Holm-adjusted contrasts against the SDK reference. In the eligible confirmatory run, overall schema validity was 0.684 and mean automated quality was 0.638. PydanticAI, LangGraph, and DSPy retained near-ceiling schema validity with mean quality 0.91-0.94, while the plain SDK, Agno, and CrewAI conditions were substantially lower in this package and model configuration. Schema-valid rows still produced many task-score flags, especially in extraction and compliance QA, and quality residuals show strong condition-by-task interactions (including a workflow collapse for CrewAI). Labelled ablations address retry budgets and feature-using mechanisms; primary contrasts remain system-configuration findings, not causal attributions to marketed library features.
